sum: English shortens words all the time; Arabic hardly does. An acronym is read as a word (NATO), an abbreviation letter by letter (ETA). Some acronyms have become ordinary words (laser, radar), and clipped forms such as lab or fax stand on their own.
pts: Classical Arabic has almost no abbreviations, apart from a few religious formulas such as بَسْمَلَ, حَوْقَلَ and صلعم.
Western-style abbreviations (ص.ب, أ.ف.ب) are recent and mostly limited to the media.
When translating an English acronym into Arabic, the safer choice is to write it out in full.
ex: ‘PO Box’
ص.ب (صُنْدُوق البَرِيد)
NATO
ناتو

sum: Both mean ‘higher than’ but are not interchangeable. ‘Above’ places something on a vertical scale; ‘over’ adds movement and is the word for numbers, quantities and measurements. Arabic normally uses فَوْقَ, and أَكْثَر مِن for numbers and amounts.
pts: Figurative ‘rise above’ and ‘get over’ (to ignore, to overcome) need verbs in Arabic such as تَجاوَزَ or تَغَلَّبَ على.
ex: “His intelligence is above average.”
ذَكاؤُهُ فَوْقَ العادَةِ
“He weighs over 75 kilograms.”
وَزْنُهُ أَكْثَرُ مِنْ 75 كيلوغراماً
“We got over our difficulties and made it through the exams.”
تَغَلَّبْنا عَلَى صِعابِنا وَنَجَحْنا في الامْتِحاناتِ

sum: There is no one-to-one match between English adverbs and Arabic forms, so the translator has to think about the type of adverbial, how many words it needs, its equivalent and where it goes in the sentence.
pts: Manner: English ‘-ly’ adverbs often become an indefinite accusative, a phrase with بِـ or في, or بِصُورة / بِشَكْلٍ / بِطَرِيقة / بِصِفة + adjective.
The most typical Arabic ways of expressing manner are the circumstantial clause (الحال) and the cognate accusative (المفعول المطلق).
Place and time: Arabic puts them after the verb or explicit subject; sentence-initial position is rare and marks emphasis.
English order is usually MANNER + PLACE + TIME; Arabic usually VERB/SUBJECT + TIME + PLACE (+ MANNER).
Frequency adverbs sit between subject and verb in English but after the verb or subject in Arabic.
ex: “They were demonstrating openly against the government.”
كانُوا يَتَظاهَرُونَ ضِدَّ الحُكُومَةِ بِطَرِيقَةٍ عَلَنِيَّةٍ
“He sat down despondently.”
جَلَسَ مُكْتَئِباً / جَلَسَ وَهُوَ مُكْتَئِبٌ
“I protested vehemently.”
لَقَدْ احْتَجَجْتُ احْتِجاجاً شَدِيداً
“The minister delivered a speech yesterday in Cairo.”
أَلْقَى الوَزِيرُ أَمْسِ مُحاضَرَةً في القاهِرَةِ

sum: ‘Advise’ is the verb, ‘advice’ the noun, and ‘advice’ is uncountable: there is no ‘advices’. Because نَصِيحة has a plural (نَصائِح), translators are tempted to write one.
pts: With a number, use ‘pieces of advice’.
English ‘advise’ takes OBJECT + TO + INFINITIVE; Arabic نَصَحَ takes أَنْ.
ex: “He gave me five pieces of advice before I left.”
وَجَّهَ لي خَمْسَ نَصائِحَ قَبْلَ مُغادَرَتي
“What would you advise me to drink after supper?”
بِمَ تَنْصَحُني أَنْ أَشْرَبَ بَعْدَ العَشاءِ؟

sum: ‘To affect’ is to have an effect on something; ‘to effect’ is to bring something about. The first is أَثَّرَ في/على; the second is usually قامَ بِـ + verbal noun.
pts: ‘Affect’ can also mean to feign or pretend: a Form VI verb (تَجاهَلَ) or تَظاهَرَ / تَصَنَّعَ / ادَّعَى / تَكَلَّفَ.
ex: “The new manager effected basic changes in this company.”
قامَ المُدِيرُ الجَدِيدُ بِإِجْراءِ تَغْيِيراتٍ أَساسِيَّةٍ في هذِهِ الشَّرِكَةِ
“He affected a headache in order not to go to the party.”
لَقَدْ تَظاهَرَ بِالصُّداعِ كَيْ لا يَذْهَبَ إِلَى الحَفْلَةِ

sum: ‘After’ is a preposition and needs an object; ‘afterwards’ is an adverb meaning ‘later’. Arabic can use بَعْدَ or بَعْدَ ذلِكَ for both, which is why learners write ‘I’ll see you after’.
pts: Arabic بَعْدَ with a stretch of time is English ‘in’: ‘in two hours’ time’, not ‘after two hours’.
ex: “I’ll see you afterwards.” (not *after)
سَأَراكَ بَعْدَ ذلِكَ
“We will go there in two hours’ time.” (not *after)
سَنَذْهَبُ إِلَى هُناكَ بَعْدَ ساعَتَيْنِ

sum: Agreement is how words change to match each other. English verbs agree only in number, and with collective nouns they follow the logical subject (the people meant), not the grammatical form. Arabic follows the grammatical subject, with its own set of exceptions.
pts: Collective nouns (government, committee, family, team) take a singular verb when the group is meant as one body and a plural verb when its members are meant.
Plural names for one entity take a singular verb: ‘The United States has…’.
Nouns of science in -ics (economics, physics, statistics) and ‘news’, ‘measles’ are singular; ‘statistics’ meaning figures is plural.
Summation plurals (scissors, trousers) take a plural verb in English but are singular nouns in Arabic: مِقَصّ, سِرْوال.
In Arabic, non-human plurals take a feminine singular verb, and a verb that comes before its subject stays singular.
Collectives for nationalities (العَرَب, الإِنْكِلِيز) are treated as masculine plural.
Dual: do not translate an English pair as a plural in Arabic; and do not carry a chain of Arabic duals into English as ‘the two…’ again and again.

Covert gender: some feminine-looking words are male (خَلِيفة, عَلّامة), and many feminine nouns carry no ة: names of women, female relatives, paired body parts, cities, most countries, and a set such as أَرْض, حَرْب, شَمْس, نار.
With quantifiers (كُلّ, بَعْض, أَغْلَب, مُعْظَم) Arabic agrees with the quantified noun; English uses a plural verb.
‘A number of’ takes a plural verb, ‘the number of’ a singular one.
Possession: English ‘leave their bags outside’ is شَنْطَتَهُم in Arabic, since each student has one bag.
ex: “The government have agreed upon a new tax increase.”
لَقَدْ وافَقَتِ الحُكُومَةُ عَلَى زِيادَةٍ جَدِيدَةٍ في الضَّرائِبِ
“The United States has decided to pull out of the Kyoto Protocol.”
قَرَّرَتِ الوِلاياتُ المُتَّحِدَةُ أَنْ تَنْسَحِبَ مِنْ مُعاهَدَةِ كِيوتو
“The men walked into the restaurant; one had a beer, whilst the other ordered a sandwich.”
دَخَلَ الرَّجُلانِ المَطْعَمَ، فَطَلَبَ أَحَدُهُما كَأْساً مِنَ العَصِيرِ في حِينِ طَلَبَ الآخَرُ شَطِيرَةً
“The lecturers left and headed for the airport.”
خَرَجَ الأَساتِذَةُ واتَّجَهُوا إِلَى المَطارِ
“They had a funny look on their faces.”
عِنْدَهُم نَظْرَةٌ مُضْحِكَةٌ عَلَى وَجْهِهِم

sum: ‘All’ can go before a plural noun with or without ‘the’; ‘all of’ needs a definite noun or a pronoun. Arabic usually uses كُلّ, which means ‘all (of)’ only before a definite plural noun or pronoun.
pts: When كُلّ is the subject of a later verb and the noun is human, the verb is plural.
Other Arabic words for totality: جَمِيع (in iḍāfa; الجَمِيع ‘everyone’; جَمِيعاً ‘all together’), أَجْمَع / بِأَجْمَعِهِ, كافّة, قاطِبة, بِأَسْرِهِ, بِرُمَّتِهِ, بِكُلِّيَّتِهِ, بِحَذافِيرِهِ.
Set phrases: ‘all in all’ (عَلَى العُمُوم), ‘all along’, ‘one and all’, ‘all alone’, ‘all the better’.
ex: “All of us attended the lecture by the Dean of the Faculty.”
حَضَرْنا كُلُّنا / جَمِيعاً المُحاضَرَةَ الَّتي أَلْقاها عَمِيدُ الكُلِّيَّةِ
“The law will be applied in its entirety.”
سَيُطَبَّقُ القانُونُ بِحَذافِيرِهِ
“All in all, I think we’re better off without him.”
عَلَى العُمُومِ نَحْنُ في وَضْعٍ أَفْضَلَ بِدُونِهِ

sum: All three give consent; the differences are grammatical. ‘Allow’ and ‘permit’ take OBJECT + TO + INFINITIVE (or -ING with no personal object); only ‘permit’ is used in the impersonal passive; only ‘allow’ takes adverb particles (‘allowed out’); ‘let’ is the least formal, takes a bare infinitive and has no passive. Arabic covers all three with سَمَحَ.
ex: “It is not permitted to eat on the premises.”
لا يُسْمَحُ بِالأَكْلِ في المَبْنَى
“The dog was not allowed out after 6 p.m.”
لَمْ يُسْمَحْ لِلْكَلْبِ بِالخُرُوجِ بَعْدَ السّاعَةِ السّادِسَةِ مَساءً
“I cannot let this happen to the company.”
لا / لَنْ أَسْمَحَ أَنْ يَحْدُثَ هذا لِلشَّرِكَةِ

sum: English uses these adverbs, usually with the present perfect; Arabic tends to express the same ideas with whole constructions and the perfect tense, and makes no difference between negative and question forms.
pts: ‘already’: (لَقَدْ) سَبَقَ لَهُ + verbal noun, or سَبَقَ لَهُ أَنْ + perfect; sometimes no adverb at all.
‘just’: لِتَوِّهِ, تَوّاً, الآن, في الحال.
‘not yet’: لَمْ + jussive + بَعْدُ.
‘already’ meaning ‘previously’: قَبْلَ الآن, قَبْلاً, سابِقاً.
‘just’ also has non-time meanings: ‘just as intelligent’ (كَـ), ‘just what I wanted to say’ (بِالضَّبْطِ), ‘I’m just so tired’ (فَقَطْ).
ex: “She has already visited the museum.”
لَقَدْ سَبَقَ لَها أَنْ زارَتِ المُتْحَفَ
“He has not come yet.”
لَمْ يَأْتِ بَعْدُ
“They have just arrived.”
وَصَلُوا لِتَوِّهِم

sum: ‘Although’ and ‘though’ both mean ‘despite’; ‘though’ is more informal, often pairs with ‘even’ and can close a sentence (meaning ‘however’); ‘albeit’ means ‘even though’ and only comes mid-sentence. Arabic offers بِالرَّغْمِ مِنْ (أَنَّ), بِرَغْمِ أَنَّ, رَغْمَ, عَلَى الرَّغْمِ مِنْ, مَعَ أَنَّ, often followed by إِلّا أَنَّ or فَـ in the main clause.
pts: فَـ is optional in the main clause except before قَدْ and إِنَّ.
ex: “He is a successful, albeit arrogant, young man.”
إِنَّهُ شابٌّ ناجِحٌ عَلَى الرَّغْمِ مِنْ تَكَبُّرِهِ
“Even though the exam was difficult, I answered all the questions.”
بِرَغْمِ أَنَّ الامْتِحانَ كانَ صَعْباً إِلّا أَنَّني أَجَبْتُ عَلَى جَمِيعِ الأَسْئِلَةِ

sum: ‘Between’ is for two, ‘among’ for three or more or a whole group. Arabic uses بَيْنَ for both (sometimes مِنْ بَيْنِ, ما بَيْنَ, فِيما بَيْنَ), and ضِمْنَ can also render ‘among’.
pts: Only ‘between’ works with time and numbers: (في) ما بَيْنَ.
ex: “I was walking among the crowd, trying desperately to find my daughter.”
كُنْتُ أَمْشي بَيْنَ حُشُودِ النّاسِ أُحاوِلُ جاهِداً أَنْ أَجِدَ ابْنَتي
“The President was among those present at the reception.”
كانَ الرَّئِيسُ مِنْ بَيْنِ الحاضِرِينَ في حَفْلَةِ الاسْتِقْبالِ
“We received between $200 and $300 for those old books.”
تَسَلَّمْنا ما بَيْنَ 200 وَ300 دُولارٍ أَمْرِيكِيٍّ لِهذِهِ الكُتُبِ القَدِيمَةِ

sum: ‘Amount’ goes with things you cannot count, ‘number’ with things you can; Arabic mirrors this with كَمِّيّة and عَدَد.
ex: “The number of cars on the road has increased dramatically over the past ten years.”
ازْدادَ عَدَدُ السَّيّاراتِ كَثِيراً في السَّنَواتِ العَشْرِ الأَخِيرَةِ

sum: These particles look alike but behave differently, and English ‘that’ covers ground that Arabic splits between أَنْ and أَنَّ.
pts: إِنَّ (one of ‘inna and her sisters’) puts its subject in the accusative and cannot be followed directly by a verb; in MSA it mostly opens a sentence as an intensifier (‘indeed’), often left untranslated.
إِنْ introduces conditional if-clauses.
أَنْ and أَنَّ both introduce ‘that’-clauses: أَنْ + subjunctive after verbs of ability, hope and expectation; أَنَّ + nominal clause after verbs of knowing and perceiving. Some verbs take both.
After قالَ, Arabic uses إِنَّ for reported speech.
لا after أَنْ contracts to أَلّا.
English can drop ‘that’; Arabic cannot drop أَنْ/أَنَّ.
An أَنْ-clause often becomes an English infinitive, and an English clause may become a phrase with a verbal noun in Arabic.
ex: “I knew that he was eager to see her.”
عَلِمْتُ أَنَّهُ مُشْتاقٌ إِلَى رُؤْيَتِها
“He swore that he would withdraw his complaint.”
أَقْسَمَ أَنْ يَسْحَبَ شَكْواهُ
“I wanted to tell her that he loved her.”
أَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَقُولَ لَها إِنَّهُ يُحِبُّها
“You must not smoke.”
يَجِبُ أَلّا تُدَخِّنَ

sum: All four signal that something has stopped. ‘Anymore’ and ‘any longer’ go with negative verbs; ‘no more’ and ‘no longer’ with affirmative ones. The usual Arabic form is the negative of عادَ: لَمْ يَعُدْ.
pts: Arabic may also use a content verb or an adverbial: بَعْدَ الآن, بَعْدَ اليَوْم, لَمْ يَبْقَ.
‘He is no more’ means he has died: تُوُفِّيَ / ماتَ.
‘Any more’ (two words) can also mean ‘not more of something’.
ex: “Polio is no longer a deadly disease.”
لَمْ يَعُدْ شَلَلُ الأَطْفالِ مَرَضاً قاتِلاً
“There is no more milk left in the fridge.”
لَمْ يَبْقَ أَيُّ حَلِيبٍ في الثَّلاجَةِ
“I can’t take his ridiculous behaviour anymore.”
لا أَسْتَطِيعُ قُبُولَ سُلُوكِهِ السَّخِيفِ بَعْدَ اليَوْمِ / بَعْدَ الآن

sum: Close in spelling, nearly opposite in meaning: ‘appeal’ attracts, ‘appal’ shocks. The usual Arabic for ‘appeal’ is أَعْجَبَ with an object pronoun; ‘appal’ usually appears in the English passive and comes out in Arabic as a participle or adjective (مُرَوِّع, مُرْعِب, مُرِيع, فَظِيع, هائِل).
ex: “The Pyramids appeal to me.”
تُعْجِبُني الأَهْرامُ
“They were appalled to discover what she had done.”
صُدِمُوا بِما اكْتَشَفُوا عَنْها
“His behaviour was appalling.”
كانَ سُلُوكُهُ مُرِيعاً

sum: Being ‘appreciative of’ something is thinking highly of it or being grateful for it; ‘appreciable’ means noticeable or clear.
ex: “Whenever I’ve spoken to her, she was always very appreciative of what I’d done for her.”
كُلَّما تَحَدَّثْتُ مَعَها وَجَدْتُها مُمْتَنَّةً لِما فَعَلْتُهُ مِنْ أَجْلِها
“There is an appreciable difference in the analysis of the data.”
هُناكَ اخْتِلافاتٌ جَلِيَّةٌ في تَحْلِيلِ البَياناتِ

sum: English often softens a ‘no’ inside a polite, almost positive frame, which rarely survives a literal translation; Arabic tends to state approval more briefly. The entry is a phrasebook of expressions graded from medium to strong.
pts: Approval, medium: ‘That seems a good idea’, ‘We’re in agreement on this issue’.
Approval, strong: ‘I couldn’t agree more’, ‘You’ve hit the nail right on the head’, ‘I’ve absolutely no objection’.
Introducing disapproval: ‘I see your point but…’, ‘I agree up to a point, but…’.
Disapproval, mild to strong: ‘That’s quite debatable’, ‘We mustn’t jump to conclusions’, ‘That’s out of the question’, ‘You’ve got it all wrong!’.
ex: “You’ve hit the nail right on the head.”
لَقَدْ أَصَبْتَ عَيْنَ الحَقِيقَةِ / لَقَدْ أَصَبْتَ المَحَزَّ
“I couldn’t agree more.”
أَنا مُوافِقٌ عَلَى ما تَقُولُ تَماماً
“I agree up to a point, but …”
أَنا أَتَّفِقُ مَعَكَ / أَنا مَعَكَ إِلَى حَدٍّ ما وَلكِنَّ …
“That’s out of the question.”
هذا الأَمْرُ غَيْرُ قابِلٍ لِلنِّقاشِ

sum: ‘Arab’ is a person of Arab origin, or anything relating to Arabs; ‘Arabic’ is only the language; ‘Arabian’ relates to the Arabian Peninsula and is never used for people. Arabic uses عَرَبِيّ for all three, though خَلِيجِيّ often renders ‘Arabian’ or ‘Gulf’.
pts: Write الخَلِيج العَرَبِيّ, and in English avoid ‘Persian Gulf’ in this context.
هُوَ خَلِيجِيّ is best translated ‘He is from the (Arabian) Gulf.’
For architecture, عَرَبِيّ is usually ‘Islamic’ in idiomatic English.
ex: “I bought an Arabic book on Islamic Spain.”
اشْتَرَيْتُ كِتاباً بِاللُّغَةِ العَرَبِيَّةِ عَنِ الأَنْدَلُسِ
“Islamic architecture spread in the Middle Ages.”
انْتَشَرَتْ هَنْدَسَةُ المِعْمارِ العَرَبِيَّةُ / العِمارَةُ الإِسْلامِيَّةُ في القُرُونِ الوُسْطَى

ar: لأنّ / بسبب / بما أنّ / نظراً لـ
sum: English introduces reasons with as, because, since, seeing that, now that, for, inasmuch as. Arabic has a wider set, each with its own grammar.
pts: إِذْ; بِسَبَبِ / بِفِعْلِ + noun or pronoun; لِأَنَّ; حَيْثُ أَنَّ / إِنَّ; إِذْ إِنَّ.
بِما أَنَّ … فَـ and نَظَراً لِـ … فَـ / فَقَدْ open the sentence with the reason.
For consequence: عَلَى ذلِكَ, لِذلِكَ, مِنْ جَرّاءِ, عَلَى ذِمَّةِ (‘for the purpose of’ an investigation).
ex: “I was late at the exam because of the rain.”
تَأَخَّرْتُ عَنِ الامْتِحانِ بِسَبَبِ المَطَرِ
“As he’s very ill, he won’t attend the meeting tomorrow.”
بِما أَنَّهُ مَرِيضٌ جِدّاً فَلَنْ يَحْضُرَ الاجْتِماعَ غَداً
“I decided to postpone my departure because of the bad weather conditions.”
نَظَراً لِسُوءِ الأَحْوالِ الجَوِّيَّةِ فَقَدْ قَرَّرْتُ تَأْجِيلَ سَفَرِي

sum: English fronts a topic with ‘as for’; Arabic marks the topic with أَمّا and the comment with فَـ, which is not translated.
pts: Arabic can also front the subject and add a resumptive pronoun; English often renders this with ‘only’.
ex: “As for the security services, they crushed the revolution without hesitation.”
أَمّا قُوّاتُ الأَمْنِ فَقَمَعَتِ الثَّوْرَةَ بِدُونِ تَرَدُّدٍ
“As for her, she will never go against her father’s wishes.”
أَمّا هِيَ فَلَنْ تُعارِضَ رَغَباتِ أَبِيها أَبَداً

sum: Both mean ‘as it would be if’ and are rendered by وَكَأَنَّ. In an unreal comparison English uses ‘were’; Arabic often uses كَما لَوْ كانَ.
ex: “It’s as if she didn’t want me to leave.”
كانَتْ وَكَأَنَّها لا تُرِيدُني أَنْ أَذْهَبَ
“They were talking about him as if he were present.”
كانُوا يَتَكَلَّمُونَ عَنْهُ كَما لَوْ كانَ حاضِراً

sum: Before a clause with a verb, English uses ‘as’; ‘like’ goes with nouns. Arabic is similar: كَـ and مِثْل before nouns, كَما (أَنَّ) before verbs.
pts: ‘He works as a painter’ (it is his job) differs from ‘He works like a painter’ (his manner), and Arabic marks the difference too.
ex: “As my mother said, you should go to the hairdresser’s.”
يَجِبُ أَنْ تَذْهَبَ إِلَى الحَلّاقِ كَما قالَتْ أُمّي
“He works as a painter.” / “He works like a painter.”
إِنَّهُ يَعْمَلُ رَسّاماً / يَعْمَلُ مِثْلَ الرَّسّامِ

sum: Arabic renders ‘as long as’ with ما دامَ, followed by a verb, noun or adverb, with the main clause often introduced by فَـ.
ex: “As long as he works for this company, his financial situation will improve.”
ما دامَ يَعْمَلُ في هذِهِ الشَّرِكَةِ، فَإِنَّ حالَتَهُ المادِّيَّةَ سَتَتَحَسَّنُ
“As long as they are in power, they are entitled to issue laws.”
ما دامُوا في الحُكْمِ يَحِقُّ لَهُم إِصْدارُ قَوانِينَ جَدِيدَةٍ

sum: ‘In the same measure as’: Arabic بِقَدْرِ ما or قَدْرَ ما + verb, or بِقَدْرِ + noun. With countable nouns English says ‘as many … as’.
ex: “I hate you as much as I love you.”
بِقَدْرِ ما أُحِبُّكِ أَكْرَهُكِ
“There are as many positive as negative aspects.”
هُناكَ إِيجابِيّاتٌ بِقَدْرِ السَّلْبِيّاتِ

ar: بمجرّد أن / حالما / ما إن… حتى
sum: English restricts the tenses here (present … future, present … present, past … past). Arabic uses بِمُجَرَّدِ أَنْ, حالَما, or the pairs ما كادَ أَنْ / لَمْ يَكَدْ / ما إِنْ … حَتَّى.
ex: “As soon as he gives me the money, I’ll give him the keys to the house.”
سَأُعْطِيهِ مِفْتاحَ البَيْتِ حالَما يُعْطِيني المالَ
“As soon as I read the letter, I realized its importance.”
ما إِنْ قَرَأْتُ الرِّسالَةَ حَتَّى أَدْرَكْتُ خُطُورَتَها

sum: ‘In addition to’, ‘not only’; with a verb it takes -ING. Arabic: إِلَى جانِبِ, فَضْلاً عَنْ, كَذلِكَ, أَيْضاً, بِالإِضافَةِ إِلَى.
pts: ‘She writes, as well as acting’ (she does both) differs from ‘She writes as well as she acts’ (equally well).
‘You might as well…’ means ‘with the same effect’: مِنَ المُسْتَحْسَنِ أَنْ.
ex: “As well as learning how to swim, he has been taking Dutch lessons.”
بِالإِضافَةِ إِلَى تَعَلُّمِهِ السِّباحَةَ فَإِنَّهُ بَدَأَ بِأَخْذِ دُرُوسٍ لِتَعَلُّمِ اللُّغَةِ الهُولَنْدِيَّةِ
“You might as well give him the photographs since I don’t need them anymore.”
مِنَ المُسْتَحْسَنِ أَنْ تُعْطِيَهُ الصُّوَرَ لِأَنَّني لَمْ أَعُدْ أَحْتاجُ إِلَيْها

sum: Arabic has a set of helper verbs that rarely stand alone and pair with a main verb, with the subject usually placed between them. They fall into groups by meaning.
pts: Inchoative (‘begin to’): أَخَذَ, أَصْبَحَ, بَدَأَ, جَعَلَ, صارَ + imperfect.

Possibility and probability: يُمْكِنُ, يَجُوزُ, يُحْتَمَلُ, يُتَوَقَّعُ, يُرَجَّحُ and مِنَ الجائِزِ / المُمْكِنِ / المُتَوَقَّعِ / المُحْتَمَلِ / المُؤَمَّلِ + أَنْ; also قَدْ + imperfect, لَعَلَّ, رُبَّما + perfect.
Imminence (‘on the point of’, ‘almost’): كادَ / يَكادُ, أَوْشَكَ / يُوشِكُ, عَلَى وَشْكِ, عَسَى. Negative كادَ means ‘barely’.
The ‘dummy’ verb قامَ بِـ + verbal noun, common in media Arabic, is ‘carried out’ or ‘effected’, and is often best left out in English.
ex: “His behaviour had begun to attract the attention of his colleagues.”
أَخَذَ سُلُوكُهُ يَسْتَرْعِي انْتِباهَ زُمَلائِهِ في الكُلِّيَّةِ
“It is probable that the crisis will continue.”
مِنَ المُحْتَمَلِ أَنْ تَسْتَمِرَّ الأَزْمَةُ
“He was on the verge of accepting the job offer.”
كانَ عَلَى وَشْكِ أَنْ يَقْبَلَ الوَظِيفَةَ
“He carried out/conducted this research.”
قامَ بِإِجْراءِ هذا البَحْثِ

sum: Both mean ‘or’, but أَمْ is preferred in questions. For ‘or not’, أَمْ لا is far more common than أَوْ لا.
pts: In English, ‘or’ comes only before the last item of a list, and ‘or not’ takes a comma.
ex: “Do you write or draw with charcoal?”
تَكْتُبُ بِالفَحْمِ أَمْ تَرْسُمُ بِهِ؟
“Did you see him, or not?”
هَلْ شاهَدْتَهُ أَمْ لا؟

sum: All four name the sea’s edge but are not interchangeable. ‘Shore’ is the general word; ‘coast’ is the wider land along the sea (maps, weather); ‘beach’ is the sandy or pebbly part; ‘seaside’ means coast and beach as a place to go. Arabic ساحِل and شاطِئ can both be ‘shore’, but only شاطِئ is ‘beach’; ‘seaside’ is often simply البَحْر.
ex: “This year, we are spending our holidays at the seaside/coast.”
نَقْضِي إِجازَتَنا هذا العامَ عَلَى البَحْرِ
“Let’s go to the beach this afternoon!”
فَلْنَذْهَبْ إِلَى الشّاطِئِ بَعْدَ ظُهْرِ اليَوْمِ

sum: Usually صارَ or أَصْبَحَ in the perfect; أَمْسَى, أَضْحَى and باتَ belong to very formal style.
pts: أَصْبَحَ, أَضْحَى and باتَ can also be content verbs (‘be in the morning’, ‘spend the night’).
Often Arabic needs no linking verb at all: كَبُرَ (become big or old), صَغُرَ, تَعَقَّدَ, نَحُفَ, سَمِنَ, طَرِشَ, سَكَتَ.
ex: “In the end, he became a very traditional artist.”
في النِّهايَةِ، صارَ فَنّاناً تَقْلِيدِيّاً جِدّاً
“I’m sure she will become a good painter.”
أَنا مُتَأَكِّدٌ مِنْ أَنَّها سَتُصْبِحُ رَسّامَةً جَيِّدَةً

sum: ‘Before’ is mostly about time (and lists, presence, set phrases); ‘in front of’ is only about place and is the opposite of ‘behind’; ‘opposite’ and ‘facing’ mean directly on the other side; ‘across’ is the other side, not necessarily directly opposite. Arabic: قَبْلَ for time and place, بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ with people, and أَمامَ, تُجاهَ, قُبالَةَ, قُدّامَ, حِيالَ, مُقابِلَ for ‘in front of’.
pts: Only ‘in front of’ can carry movement.
‘Across’ as ‘from one side to the other’: نَحْوَ, فَوْقَ, عَلَى, مِنْ جانِبٍ إِلَى آخَرَ, عَبْرَ.
ex: “The building across the street has been broken into twice this week.”
اقْتُحِمَتِ البِنايَةُ الَّتي تَقَعُ مُقابِلَ الشّارِعِ مَرَّتَيْنِ هذا الأُسْبُوعَ
“He ran across the street to see what was going on.”
رَكَضَ إِلَى الجانِبِ الآخَرِ مِنَ الشّارِعِ لِمَعْرِفَةِ ما يَجْرِي

sum: ‘Below’ is the opposite of ‘above’ (a lower level); ‘under’ and ‘beneath’ mean directly under, ‘beneath’ with some distance; ‘underneath’ adds touching or covering. ‘Under’ is preferred in abstract senses. Arabic uses تَحْتَ (or أَسْفَلَ), and دُونَ for rank, value and age.
ex: “The city centre came under the control of armed gangs.”
أَصْبَحَ وَسَطُ المَدِينَةِ تَحْتَ سَيْطَرَةِ العِصاباتِ المُسَلَّحَةِ
“The occupying authority refused entry to the mosque to worshippers below the age of fifty.”
تَمْنَعُ السُّلُطاتُ المُحْتَلَّةُ المُصَلِّينَ دُونَ سِنِّ الخَمْسِينَ مِنْ دُخُولِ المَسْجِدِ

sum: ‘Beside’ means ‘next to’ (بِجانِبِ); ‘besides’ means ‘in addition’, like ‘moreover’: أَيْضاً, فِيما عَدا ذلِكَ, بِالإِضافَةِ إِلَى, وَفَوْقَ ذلِكَ, عِلاوَةً عَلَى, إِلَى جانِبِ, فَضْلاً عَنْ.
ex: “Why don’t you want to sit beside your brother?”
لِماذا لا تُرِيدُ أَنْ تَجْلِسَ إِلَى جِوارِ أَخِيكَ؟
“I don’t enjoy painting. Besides, I was never good at it.”
لا أَسْتَمْتِعُ بِالرَّسْمِ، وَعِلاوَةً عَلَى ذلِكَ، لَمْ أُحْسِنْهُ عَلَى الإِطْلاقِ

sum: ‘Great’ is for abstract things (very good, magnificent); ‘big’ and ‘large’ mean the same, ‘large’ being more formal. Arabic: كَبِير for big/large, عَظِيم for great.
pts: Arabic كَبِير often means old (short for كَبِيرُ السِّنّ), while English ‘big’ can mean fat (سَمِين).
كَبِير as the first term of an iḍāfa with a plural is ‘chief’ or ‘head’: كَبِيرُ الأَطِبّاءِ ‘head physician’.
ex: “He came up with a great idea to save the company.”
طَرَحَ فِكْرَةً عَظِيمَةً لِإِنْقاذِ الشَّرِكَةِ
“He is an old man and therefore deserves our respect.”
هذا الرَّجُلُ كَبِيرٌ وَيَسْتَحِقُّ احْتِرامَنا

sum: ‘Border’ and ‘frontier’ both name the line between countries, but today ‘border’ covers customs and passports and ‘frontier’ is mostly figurative (limits); ‘boundary’ marks smaller areas. Arabic حُدُود covers all; تُخُوم cannot be used for a border with customs. The Arabic plural is often an English singular.
ex: “We crossed the border at midnight.”
عَبَرْنا الحُدُودَ عِنْدَ مُنْتَصَفِ اللَّيْلِ
“Our University is trying to push back the frontiers of science.”
تُحاوِلُ جامِعَتُنا أَنْ تُوَسِّعَ آفاقَ العِلْمِ

sum: Use ‘both’ only for two, and keep the grammar parallel, especially with prepositions (‘interested in both history and French’ or ‘both in history and in French’). Arabic uses كِلا / كِلْتا with a definite dual or a pronoun suffix; it agrees in gender but not in case.
pts: مَعَ كِلَيْهِما (together) differs from مَعَ كُلٍّ مِنْهُما (each separately), a nuance English ‘both’ loses.
‘Both’ is negated with ‘neither’.
ex: “He grabbed the book with both hands.”
لَقَدْ أَمْسَكَ الكِتابَ بِكِلْتا يَدَيْهِ
“Did you see both cars? No, I saw neither!”
هَلْ رَأَيْتَ كِلْتا السَّيّارَتَيْنِ؟ لا، لَمْ أَرَ أَيّاً مِنْهُما!

sum: ‘Bring’ is movement towards the speaker or listener, ‘take’ movement away. ‘Bring’: أَتَى بِـ, أَحْضَرَ, حَمَلَ إِلَى, جَلَبَ, جاءَ بِـ; ‘take’: أَخَذَ, حَمَلَ إِلَى.
pts: ‘Take back’ needs its own verb: اسْتَرْجَعَ, اسْتَرَدَّ, اسْتَعادَ, أَعادَ.
ex: “After I was brought before the manager, I was taken to the meeting room.”
بَعْدَ أَنْ أَحْضَرُوني إِلَى المُدِيرِ، أَخَذُوني إِلَى قاعَةِ الاجْتِماعاتِ
“Saladin took Jerusalem back from the Franks.”
اسْتَرْجَعَ صَلاحُ الدِّينِ الأَيُّوبِيُّ القُدْسَ مِنْ أَيْدِي الإِفْرَنْجِ

sum: ‘By’ names the method or means (and modes of transport); ‘with’ names the tool. Arabic: بِـ, بِطَرِيقة, بِواسِطة, عَنْ طَرِيق, عَبْرَ, مِنْ خِلالِ; plain بِـ is the most common.
ex: “We travelled by plane/car/bus/bicycle.”
سافَرْنا بِالطّائِرَةِ / بِالسَّيّارَةِ / بِالباصِ / بِالدَّرّاجَةِ
“The soldier was killed with a knife.”
لَقَدْ قُتِلَ الجُنْدِيُّ بِسِكِّينٍ

sum: These modals express possibility and doubt. Strictly, ‘can’ is ability, ‘may’ possibility or permission, and ‘might’ a more remote possibility; in current English ‘can’ also covers permission and possibility. Arabic separates them: ability with اسْتَطاعَ, القُدْرة عَلَى; possibility with يُمْكِنُ أَنْ, لَعَلَّ, رُبَّما, قَدْ + imperfect; permission with يُمْكِنُكَ, يَجُوزُ لَكَ.
pts: The book lists thirteen Arabic ways of saying ‘The teacher may be in his office’ (مِنَ المُمْكِنِ أَنْ, يُمْكِنُ أَنْ, يَجُوزُ أَنْ, مِنَ الجائِزِ أَنْ, يُرَجَّحُ أَنْ, مِنَ المُرَجَّحِ أَنَّ, مِنَ / عَلَى الأَرْجَحِ أَنْ, مِنَ المُحْتَمَلِ أَنْ, يُحْتَمَلُ أَنْ, رُبَّما, رُبَّما أَنَّ, عَسَى أَنْ, عَسَى أَنَّ); some of them signal probability.
‘Might’ is also the past of ‘may’ (possibility) and replaces it in reported speech; past permission is ‘was allowed’.
Negation shifts meaning: ‘He can’t have known’ (impossible) versus ‘He may not have known’ (uncertain).
‘Might’ is typically قَدْ + imperfect.
ex: “You can’t play such loud music in the middle of the night; the neighbours will call the police!”
لا يُمْكِنُكَ / يَجُوزُ لَكَ أَنْ تَعْزِفَ مُوسِيقَى صاخِبَةً في مُنْتَصَفِ اللَّيْلِ وَإِلّا سَيَقُومُ الجِيرانُ بِاسْتِدْعاءِ الشُّرْطَةِ!
“He may not have known about her secret.”
رُبَّما لَمْ يَكُنْ يَعْلَمُ بِسِرِّها
“He may come over to our house tomorrow evening.”
قَدْ يَأْتِي إِلَى مَنْزِلِنا مَساءَ غَدٍ

sum: A ‘canal’ is man-made, a ‘channel’ natural; Arabic قَناة covers both (تُرْعة is a drainage canal). Only ‘channel’ is used for television (قَناة or قَنال); radio has ‘stations’, also قَناة (إِذاعِيّة).
pts: Proper names: القَناةُ الإِنْكِلِيزِيَّةُ ‘the English Channel’, قَناةُ السُّوَيْسِ ‘the Suez Canal’.
ex: “Each of the three radio stations can broadcast to both the Middle East and Europe.”
يُمْكِنُ لِكُلِّ قَناةٍ مِنَ القَنَواتِ الإِذاعِيَّةِ الثَّلاثِ أَنْ تَبُثَّ إِلَى الشَّرْقِ الأَوْسَطِ وَأُورُوبّا

sum: ‘Classic’ means first-rate, typical, or always in fashion (and as a noun, a work of the highest excellence); ‘the Classics’ are great literature, and ‘Classics’ is the study of Greece and Rome; ‘classicism’ is the ideas of Greek and Roman antiquity or an 18th-century style; ‘classical’ means of antiquity, ‘serious’ music, or traditional in science and art.
pts: Arabic prefers the borrowing كلاسيكي in cultural contexts; otherwise مُمْتاز, رائِع, نَمَطِيّ, تَقْلِيدِيّ.
ex: “a classic mistake”
خَطَأٌ نَمَطِيٌّ / مُتَوَقَّعٌ
“classical economic theory”
نَظَرِيَّةٌ اقْتِصادِيَّةٌ تَقْلِيدِيَّةٌ

sum: Often interchangeable, but ‘shut’ is more informal and cannot stand before a noun (‘a closed door’, not ‘a shut door’), nor be used of roads or companies.
ex: “Don’t forget to close/shut the door.”
لا تَنْسَ أَنْ تُغْلِقَ البابَ / تُقْفِلَ البابَ
“The factory closed (down) last year.”
لَقَدْ أَوْقَفَ المَعْمَلُ أَعْمالَهُ العامَ الماضِي

sum: ‘Common’ is shared (in common); ‘joint’ is combined effort. Arabic uses مُشْتَرَك for both. ‘Jointly responsible’ is تَضامَنَ.
pts: Do not confuse this with ‘common’ meaning usual (عادِيّ, شائِع, مَأْلُوف), or its pejorative sense ‘vulgar’ (غَيْرُ مُتَحَضِّر).
ex: “Our common goal is to become the best in the field.”
هَدَفُنا المُشْتَرَكُ هُوَ أَنْ نُصْبِحَ الأَفْضَلَ في هذا المَجالِ
“This is a common view which many people would agree with.”
هذِهِ وِجْهَةُ نَظَرٍ عادِيَّةٌ / شائِعَةٌ يَتَّفِقُ مَعَها الكَثِيرُ مِنَ النّاسِ

sum: English has inflected forms (kinder, fastest) and ‘more/most’ + adjective; the latter is for longer words and for adjectives after the noun, and idiom should decide. Arabic uses the elative أَفْعَل + مِنْ (no agreement), or أَكْثَر / أَشَدّ / أَقَلّ + an accusative verbal noun when the adjective cannot take the elative pattern.
pts: Colour and defect adjectives already in أَفْعَل form (أَصْلَع) agree in gender and number and have no comparative meaning.
خَيْر and شَرّ carry comparative meaning: ‘better’, ‘worse’.
Comparing two qualities of the same person needs a resumptive pronoun after مِنْ.
Equality: كَـ, مِثْل, عَلَى قَدْر, بِقَدْر.
The superlative is always definite (article, suffix, or iḍāfa); the feminine and plural forms survive mainly in set names: بِرِيطانيا العُظْمَى, القُرُونُ الوُسْطَى, الشَّرْقُ الأَوْسَطُ.
‘The more … the more’ is كُلَّما … كُلَّما + perfect; do not confuse it with كُلّ ما ‘all of’.
ex: “Prevention is better than cure.”
الوِقايَةُ خَيْرٌ مِنْ أَلْفِ عِلاجٍ
“The responsibility appears to be more important and more complicated than before.”
تَبْدُو المَسْؤُولِيَّةُ أَكْبَرَ وَأَكْثَرَ تَعْقِيداً مِنْ ذِي قَبْلٍ
“The dolphin is the most intelligent marine animal.”
الدُّلْفِينُ هُوَ أَذْكَى حَيَوانٍ بَحْرِيٍّ
“The more you study, the greater your chances of succeeding.”
كُلَّما دَرَسْتَ كُلَّما زادَتْ فُرَصُ نَجاحِكَ

sum: Both languages fix the tenses of the if-clause (protasis, شَرْط) and the result (apodosis, جَواب). The choice depends on whether the condition is real, possible, or impossible because it lies in the past.
pts: Type I (real possibility): English present + future; Arabic إِذا / إِنْ + perfect (or imperfect), result with or without سَـ / سَوْفَ.
Type II (non-past hypothesis): English past + would; Arabic لَوْ + perfect, with لَـ introducing the result.
Type III (past, impossible): English past perfect + would have; Arabic لَوْ كانَ قَدْ + perfect, with لَـ.
If the result comes first in Arabic, لَـ and فَـ drop; إِذا takes فَـ before an imperative.
Negation: لَوْ لَمْ / لَوْ أَنَّ … لَما; وَإِلّا ‘or else, otherwise’; لَوْلا (أَنَّ) + noun ‘were it not for’.
Some Arabic conditionals are not translated as such: إِنْ شاءَ اللهُ is ‘God willing’, not ‘if God wills’.
Arabic prefers the perfect in conditions even where English uses present or future.
ex: If I DID this, I WOULD SUCCEED.
لَوْ عَمِلْتُ ذلِكَ لَنَجَحْتُ
If I HAD DONE this, I WOULD HAVE SUCCEEDED.
لَوْ كُنْتُ قَدْ عَمِلْتُ ذلِكَ لَنَجَحْتُ
“If I hadn’t been ill, I would have come along with you.”
لَوْلا المَرَضُ (لَوْ لَمْ أَكُنْ مَرِيضاً) لَسافَرْتُ مَعَكَ
“We must reconsider our position, if not we’ll lose the deal.”
عَلَيْنا أَنْ نُعِيدَ النَّظَرَ في المَوْضُوعِ، وَإِلّا فَسَنَخْسَرُ الصَّفْقَةَ

sum: ‘Confident’ is self-assured (واثِق, عَلَى ثِقَة); ‘confidential’ is secret (سِرِّيّ); a ‘confidant’ is the person you tell your secrets to (نَجِيّ).
ex: “He is confident that hard work will yield the desired results.”
إِنَّهُ عَلَى ثِقَةٍ مِنْ أَنَّ العَمَلَ الشّاقَّ سَوْفَ يُحَقِّقُ النَّتائِجَ المَرْجُوَّةَ
“This is very confidential information that should not leave this company.”
هذِهِ المَعْلُوماتُ سِرِّيَّةٌ لِلْغايَةِ وَيَنْبَغِي أَلّا تَتَسَرَّبَ خارِجَ هذِهِ الشَّرِكَةِ

sum: ‘Conscious’ is awake, or aware (of); ‘consciousness’ is being alert; ‘conscience’ is the sense of right and wrong (ضَمِير); ‘conscientious’ is diligent.
pts: فَقَدَ الوَعْيَ ‘to faint’; اسْتَعادَ وَعْيَهُ ‘to come round’; الوَعْيُ القَوْمِيُّ ‘national consciousness’; اللّاوَعْي ‘the unconscious’; عَنْ غَيْرِ وَعْيٍ ‘unconsciously’.
ex: “I’m very conscious of the fact that we need to adopt a new sales policy.”
أَنا مُدْرِكٌ تَماماً / واعٍ جِدّاً الحَقِيقَةَ أَنَّنا في حاجَةٍ لِتَبَنِّي سِياسَةٍ جَدِيدَةٍ لِلْمَبِيعاتِ
“One should always be guided by one’s conscience when making decisions in life.”
يَجِبُ عَلَى المَرْءِ أَنْ يُراجِعَ ضَمِيرَهُ دائِماً عِنْدَ اتِّخاذِ القَراراتِ في الحَياةِ

sum: ‘Contemptible’ deserves contempt; ‘contemptuous (of)’ shows it. Arabic marks the difference with passive and active participles.
ex: “He really is a contemptible fellow.”
إِنَّهُ حَقّاً شَخْصٌ حَقِيرٌ / مُحْتَقَرٌ
“She was contemptuous of my actions.”
كانَتْ مُحْتَقِرَةً / مُزْدَرِيَةً لِأَفْعالي

sum: ‘Continual’ repeats with breaks; ‘continuous’ has no break; ‘continuation’ is the carrying on of an activity; ‘continuance’ is duration (and, in US law, an adjournment); ‘continuity’ is an unbroken link. Arabic usually draws on اسْتَمَرَّ and تَواصَلَ.
ex: “We continually tried to call the club chairman.”
حاوَلْنا مِراراً أَنْ نَتَّصِلَ بِمُدِيرِ النّادِي
“The Judge granted a continuance to the defence lawyer so that he could interview more witnesses.”
مَنَحَ القاضِي مُحامِيَ الدِّفاعِ مُدَّةً أَطْوَلَ لِيَسْتَمِرَّ في اسْتِجْوابِ المَزِيدِ مِنَ الشُّهُودِ

sum: A ‘conversation’ is a discussion: حِوار, مُكالَمة on the phone, حَدِيث (also ‘interview’). ‘Conversant with’ means familiar with: مُطَّلِع عَلَى, واقِف عَلَى, مُلِمّ بِـ, ماهِر بِـ, خَبِير في.
ex: “During the interview, the journalist severely criticized the minister.”
انْتَقَدَ الصَّحَفِيُّ الوَزِيرَ انْتِقاداً لاذِعاً خِلالَ الحَدِيثِ
“You don’t need to give her any explanation since she is conversant with the principles of mechanical engineering.”
إِنَّها لا تَحْتاجُ إِلَى أَيِّ تَفْسِيرٍ إِذْ أَنَّها مُطَّلِعَةٌ عَلَى مَبادِئِ الهَنْدَسَةِ المِيكانِيكِيَّةِ

sum: Many Arabic particles come in two parts, with a second element that must appear later in the sentence; English rarely works this way, so the second part is easy to drop or to over-translate.
pts: أَ … أَمْ; إِذا … فَـ; إِلَى جانِبِ ذلِكَ … (فَـ); أَمّا … فَـ; إِمّا … أَوْ / وَإِمّا (‘either … or’).
إِنْ / أَيْنَما / حَيْثُما … فَـ; بِالرَّغْمِ مِنْ / بِرَغْمِ / رَغْمَ (أَنَّ) … (فَـ); بِما أَنَّ … فَإِنَّ; بَيْنَ … وَبَيْنَ.
سَواءٌ … أَمْ / أَوْ (‘whether … or’); لا … وَلا (‘neither … nor’); لا … إِلّا (‘nothing except’); لَيْسَ … إِلّا, ما … إِلّا (‘nothing but’).
لا … فَحَسْبُ / فَقَطْ بَلْ … أَيْضاً (‘not only … but also’); لَمْ / لَنْ … وَلا; لَوْ … لَـ / فَـ / سَوْفَ / قَدْ.
ما إِنْ / ما أَنْ … حَتَّى (‘no sooner … than’); ما هِيَ إِلّا … حَتَّى; مَهْما … فَـ; مَعَ أَنَّ … فَـ / إِلّا أَنَّ; نَظَراً لِـ … فَـ.
ex: “Either you pay the fine, or you’ll have to go to jail.”
إِمّا أَنْ تَدْفَعَ الغَرامَةَ أَوْ تَدْخُلَ السِّجْنَ
“Naguib Mahfouz’s novels are famous not just in the Middle East, but all over the whole world.”
إِنَّ رِواياتِ نَجِيب مَحْفُوظ مَشْهُورَةٌ لَيْسَ في الشَّرْقِ الأَوْسَطِ فَحَسْبُ بَلْ في جَمِيعِ أَنْحاءِ العالَمِ أَيْضاً
“No sooner did he see me, than he greeted me.”
ما إِنْ رَآني حَتَّى سَلَّمَ عَلَيَّ
“This is nothing but wastage.”
ما هذا إِلّا مِياهُ الصَّرْفِ

sum: ‘Credible’ is believable (مُصَدَّق, مَوْثُوق); ‘creditable’ is praiseworthy (مَشْكُور, فاضِل, مَحْمُود, حَمِيد). The negative of ‘credible’ is ‘incredible’, but ‘creditable’ can only be ‘not creditable’.
ex: “These words are neither convincing nor credible.”
هذا الكَلامُ غَيْرُ مُقْنِعٍ وَغَيْرُ مُصَدَّقٍ
“Everything was satisfactory thanks to the creditable individual efforts.”
كُلُّ شَيْءٍ كانَ عَلَى ما يُرامُ بِفَضْلِ الجُهُودِ المَشْكُورَةِ لِبَعْضِ الأَفْرادِ

sum: ‘Criticism’ is disapproval (نَقْد); a ‘critic’ evaluates books and plays (ناقِد, pl. نُقّاد); a ‘critique’ is a critical review or academic article; ‘critical’ means crucial (حاسِم, حَرِج, فاصِل) or negative, usually with ‘of’ (انْتِقادِيّ).
ex: “This is the company that faced formidable challenges in a critical economic phase.”
هذِهِ هِيَ المُؤَسَّسَةُ الَّتي واجَهَتْ تَحَدِّياتٍ عَظِيمَةً في مَرْحَلَةٍ اقْتِصادِيَّةٍ حَرِجَةٍ
“The newspaper was critical of the decision made by the previous government.”
كانَتِ الجَرِيدَةُ انْتِقادِيَّةً / مُنْتَقِدَةً لِقَرارِ الحُكُومَةِ السّابِقَةِ

sum: ‘Cry’ can mean shout or scream (often ‘cry out’) or shed tears; ‘weep’ is the formal word for the second; ‘shout’ is simply speaking very loudly; ‘sob’ is crying in short bursts.
pts: to cry, weep: بَكَى (عَلَى); to shout, cry out: صاحَ, زَعَقَ, صَرَخَ (often for help), هَتَفَ (often for joy); to sob: نَهْنَهَ, شَهَقَ, نَشَجَ, نَحَبَ, انْتَحَبَ.
Set phrases: أَجْهَشَ بِالبُكاءِ ‘to break into sobs’, بَكَى بُكاءً مُرّاً ‘to cry bitterly’, بَكَى بِدُمُوعِ التِّمْساحِ ‘crocodile tears’.
Figurative: ‘crying out for’ (في أَمَسِّ الحاجَةِ إِلَى), ‘cry off’ (cancel), ‘shout down’, ‘shout out’.
ex: “He saw his father sobbing, the tears rolling down his cheeks.”
رَأَى أَباهُ يَنْشِجُ وَدُمُوعُهُ تَتَساقَطُ عَلَى وَجْنَتَيْهِ
“This car is crying out to be cleaned!”
إِنَّ السَّيّارَةَ في أَمَسِّ الحاجَةِ إِلَى التَّنْظِيفِ

sum: ‘Dare’ is to have the courage or take the risk: تَجَرَّأَ عَلَى, جَرُؤَ عَلَى, جَسَرَ عَلَى, تَجاسَرَ عَلَى. As a modal (like ‘need’) it has one form and appears in negatives and questions. ‘I dare say’ (first person only) means ‘I suppose’.
ex: “When you come back, no-one will dare to behave in this way.”
حِينَ تَعُودُ لا يَجْرُؤُ أَحَدٌ عَلَى التَّصَرُّفِ بِهذِهِ الطَّرِيقَةِ
“He daren’t visit his friend.”
لا يَجْسُرُ عَلَى زِيارَةِ صَدِيقِهِ

sum: ‘Definite’ is certain or clear; ‘definitive’ is final. Arabic قاطِع or قَطْعِيّ can render both, and مُحَدَّد also works for ‘definite’.
ex: “It is necessary for the judge to render a definitive judgement in this matter.”
إِنَّهُ مِنَ الضَّرُورِيِّ أَنْ يُصْدِرَ القاضِي حُكْمَهُ النِّهائِيَّ / القاطِعَ في هذِهِ القَضِيَّةِ
“The government has a definite responsibility.”
هُناكَ مَسْؤُولِيَّةٌ مُحَدَّدَةٌ أَمامَ الحُكُومَةِ

sum: ‘Dependent (on)’ is the adjective; a ‘dependant’ is a person who relies on someone for support. Arabic uses عَوَّلَ عَلَى for sustenance (hence عائِلة, عِيال) and اعْتَمَدَ عَلَى in general.
pts: Do not render ‘independent’ and ‘independence’ automatically as مُسْتَقِلّ, اسْتِقْلال; that is right only in politics. In the sense of self-sufficient: غَيْرُ مُعَوِّلٍ عَلَى, مُكْتَفٍ ذاتِيّاً.
‘dependence on’, ‘independent of’, ‘independence from’.
ex: “The factory relies on ethylene oxide and ammonia for its production.”
يَعْتَمِدُ المَصْنَعُ في إِنْتاجِهِ عَلَى أُوكْسِيدِ الإِيثِيلِين وَالأَمُونْيا
“The scholar created the theory independent of philosophy.”
كانَ الباحِثُ يُبْدِعُ غَيْرَ مُعَوِّلٍ عَلَى الفَلْسَفَةِ

sum: ‘Disinterested’ is impartial (نَزاهة); ‘uninterested’ is indifferent (لا مُبالاة, عَدَمُ الاهْتِمام).
ex: “A disinterested judiciary is the only guarantee for freedom in public life.”
نَزاهَةُ القُضاةِ هِيَ الضَّمانَةُ الوَحِيدَةُ لِلْحُرِّيَّةِ في الحَياةِ العامَّةِ
“It is clear he is completely uninterested in this initiative.”
واضِحٌ أَنَّهُ غَيْرُ مُهْتَمٍّ بَتاتاً بِهذِهِ المُبادَرَةِ

sum: ‘Distinct’ is clear or separate; ‘distinctive’ is what marks something out. Arabic: مُتَمَيِّز, مُبِين, مُمَيِّز.
ex: “Does she have any distinctive features?”
هَلْ تَتَمَتَّعُ هِيَ بِصِفاتٍ مُمَيِّزَةٍ؟

sum: ‘Disused’ is no longer used; ‘misused’ used the wrong way; ‘abuse’ is maltreatment, injury or insult. ‘To fall into disuse’ is بَطَلَ, تَعَطَّلَ or عُطِّلَ.
ex: “Misuse of the equipment constitutes a health hazard.”
إِنَّ سُوءَ اسْتِعْمالِ / اسْتِخْدامِ الجِهازِ يُضِرُّ بِالصِّحَّةِ
“EU Ministers are set to impose sanctions over human rights abuses.”
بَدَأَ وُزَراءُ الاتِّحادِ الأُورُوبِيِّ العَمَلَ لِفَرْضِ عُقُوباتٍ بِشَأْنِ انْتِهاكاتِ حُقُوقِ الإِنْسانِ

sum: ‘In’ says when; ‘during’ stresses duration or an activity; ‘for’ says how long; ‘since’ marks the starting point (مُنْذُ). Arabic has a range: إِبّانَ, في (أَثْناءِ), خِلالَ, طِوالَ, طِيلَةَ, في غُضُونِ, في مُدَّة, عَلَى مَدارِ, مَدَى.
pts: طِوال and طِيلة stress continuity; إِبّانَ, في and أَثْناءَ are not used with specific numbers, في مُدَّة mostly is.
مُنْذُ is ‘since’ for a starting point and ‘for’ for a period, and both need the English present perfect: not *‘He is a teacher since 1999’ but ‘He has been a teacher since 1999’.
ex: “He has worked here for five years.”
يَعْمَلُ هُنا مُنْذُ خَمْسِ سَنَواتٍ
“during the war for the liberation of Kuwait”
في / إِبّانَ حَرْبِ التَّحْرِيرِ لِلْكُوَيْتِ
“I have lived here for (NOT since!) three years.”
عِشْتُ هُنا مُنْذُ ثَلاثَةِ أَعْوامٍ

sum: ‘Each’ looks at members one by one, ‘every’ at the whole group; only ‘each’ can take ‘of’ or follow a subject. Arabic uses كُلّ for both, often with مِنْ.
ex: “Each of them is totally different from the other.”
كُلٌّ مِنْهُما يَخْتَلِفُ تَماماً عَنِ الآخَرِ
“The students each handed in their assignments.”
سَلَّمَ كُلُّ طالِبٍ وَظِيفَتَهُ / واجِبَهُ

sum: The two are interchangeable in English (the two-versus-many rule is a myth). Arabic expresses reciprocity with a Form VI verb (تَحارَبَ) or with بَعْض … بَعْضاً / بَعْض.
pts: بَعْضاً is used only when the verb has no preposition; with a preposition, the preposition follows the verb directly: انْضَمَّ بَعْضُهُم إِلَى بَعْضٍ.
Media Arabic sometimes writes بَعْضُها البَعْض.
Modern Arabic often adds the pronoun even with Form VI verbs; and some English verbs are already reciprocal, so ‘each other’ can be dropped.
ex: “They wrote to each other every day.”
كانُوا يَتَراسَلُونَ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ
“We understand each other/one another.”
نَفْهَمُ بَعْضُنا بَعْضاً
“These words contradict each other.”
هذِهِ الكَلِماتُ تَتَناقَضُ بَعْضُها بَعْضاً

sum: Strictly, ‘eatable’ is food in a fit state to be eaten and ‘edible’ is food fit for humans at all, though the two have blurred; only ‘edibles’ has a plural. Arabic keeps a similar split: قابِل لِلْأَكْل for eatable, صالِح لِلْأَكْل for edible.
ex: “He said that the lamb (meat) was sound and eatable.”
قالَ إِنَّ لَحْمَ الأَغْنامِ سَلِيمٌ وَصالِحٌ لِلْأَكْلِ

sum: ‘Economic’ relates to the economy; ‘economical’ saves time or money. Both are usually اقْتِصادِيّ; ‘economical’ is sometimes simply رَخِيص.
ex: “The reader will find a list of the ten most economical cars on the next page.”
يَجِدُ القارِئُ في الصَّفْحَةِ التّالِيَةِ قائِمَةً بِأَفْضَلِ 10 سَيّاراتٍ اقْتِصادِيَّةٍ
“What is the most economical way of travel?”
ما أَرْخَصُ طَرِيقَةٍ لِلسَّفَرِ؟

sum: ‘Effective’ produces an effect (فاعِل, فَعّال, فَعّالِيّة); ‘efficient’ avoids waste (better كُفْء or مُقْتَدِر); ‘efficacious’ is a formal ‘effective’.
ex: “Aspirin is an effective drug against headaches.”
الأَسْبِرِينُ دَواءٌ فَعّالٌ ضِدَّ الصُّداعِ
“This is the most fuel efficient car.”
هذِهِ السَّيّارَةُ الأَكْثَرُ كَفاءَةً في اسْتِهْلاكِ الوَقُودِ

sum: Like ‘both’, ‘either’ is for two only and takes a singular verb in formal writing. ‘Either … or’ is إِمّا … أَوْ / وَإِمّا (sometimes plain أَوْ); ‘either of’ is أَيٌّ مِنْ or أَحَدُ … مِنْ; ‘neither … nor’ is usually لا … وَلا; ‘neither one’ is أَحَد.
pts: For more than two options English uses commas and one ‘or’; Arabic repeats أَوْ before each.
Arabic لا … وَلا can run to any number of items, so English may need rephrasing.
In negative sentences ‘either’ means ‘also’: ‘I haven’t met him either’ (لَمْ أُقابِلْهُ أَيْضاً).
ex: “Either victory or death!”
إِمّا النَّصْرُ وَإِمّا المَوْتُ
“Neither the Hebron nor the Oslo agreement has been implemented.”
لَمْ تُنَفَّذِ اتِّفاقِيَّةُ الخَلِيلِ وَلا اتِّفاقُ أُوسْلُو
“Neither (one) of us can ride the horse.”
لَيْسَ في اسْتِطاعَةِ أَحَدِنا أَنْ يَرْكَبَ الخَيْلَ

sum: ‘Migrate’ is the general word; ‘emigrate’ is leaving a place, ‘immigrate’ arriving: one country’s emigrant is another’s immigrant. Arabic نَزَحَ (نازِح) is general; هاجَرَ (مُهاجِر) is strictly emigration but now covers both.
pts: هِجْرة (emigration) and مَهْجَر (place of emigration) suggest exile; هِجْرة can be ‘flight’; المَهْجَر is the (Arab) diaspora; هِجْرَةُ العُقُول is ‘brain drain’.
ex: “He was born in Poland and emigrated as a child to France.”
وُلِدَ في بُولَنْدا وَهاجَرَ صَغِيراً إِلَى فَرَنْسا
“The Romantic movement was a revolution and its leaders were authors in the (Arab) diaspora.”
الحَرَكَةُ الرُّومانْتِيكِيَّةُ ثَوْرَةٌ وَرُوّادُها أُدَباءُ المَهْجَرِ

sum: ‘Ensure’ (US ‘insure’) is close to guarantee and takes a clause; ‘insure’ is protection against risk or loss; ‘assure’ is the traditional British word for life cover, though ‘life insurance’ is spreading. Arabic covers insurance with أَمَّنَ / تَأْمِين.
ex: “Every individual is entitled to treatment under the national health insurance scheme.”
لِكُلِّ فَرْدٍ الحَقُّ في العِلاجِ طِبْقاً لِنِظامِ التَّأْمِينِ الصِّحِّيِّ الوَطَنِيِّ
“… in order to ensure/guarantee the supply of electricity for all uses.”
… بِهَدَفِ تَأْمِينِ / تَزْوِيدِ الطّاقَةِ الكَهْرَبائِيَّةِ لِكافَّةِ الاسْتِخْداماتِ

sum: ‘Even’ is حَتَّى, with the next noun in the same case as the one before it; حَتَّى never takes a suffix. ‘Even if’ is hypothetical, ‘even though’ factual; Arabic covers both with حَتَّى وَإِنْ, حَتَّى إِذا, حَتَّى لَوْ, وَإِنْ, وَلَوْ, وَإِنْ كانَ, usually with the perfect.
pts: These forms can also mean ‘if only’.
‘Even so’ (yet, nevertheless): مَعَ أَنَّ, رَغْمَ, بِالرَّغْمِ مِنْ ذلِكَ, or simply لكِنَّ.
ex: “She took everything, even the car.”
أَخَذَتْ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ حَتَّى السَّيّارَةَ
“I shall not say anything, even if they torture me.”
لَنْ أَقُولَ أَيَّ شَيْءٍ وَلَوْ عَذَّبُوني
“I want to visit my mother in hospital, if only for an hour.”
أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَزُورَ أُمّي في المُسْتَشْفَى حَتَّى وَلَوْ لِساعَةٍ واحِدَةٍ

sum: ‘Ever’ is at any time, ‘never’ at no time; ‘never’ goes with affirmative verbs, ‘ever’ mostly with negatives and questions, usually with the present perfect. Arabic uses أَبَداً, قَطُّ, كَلّا, عَلَى الإِطْلاقِ, مُطْلَقاً with negative verbs.
pts: قَطُّ goes with past tenses, أَبَداً with present and especially future.
Superlatives take ‘ever’, not ‘never’: ‘the most terrible thing I have ever seen’.
ex: “He has never been outside his village in South Lebanon.”
لَمْ يَخْرُجْ مِنْ قَرْيَتِهِ في جَنُوبِ لُبْنانَ قَطُّ
“I will never ever forget this.”
لَنْ أَنْسَى ذلِكَ أَبَداً
“This is the most terrible thing I have ever seen.”
هذا أَفْظَعُ ما شاهَدْتُهُ عَلَى الإِطْلاقِ

sum: ‘Everyone’, ‘no one’, ‘somebody’ and the like take a singular verb; ‘every one’ means every single one. Arabic: كُلّ مِنْ, كُلُّ واحِدٍ, جَمِيعاً.
ex: “Every one of them took his share.”
أَخَذَ كُلُّ واحِدٍ نَصِيبَهُ
“Every one of the workers went on strike.”
قامَ جَمِيعُ / كُلُّ العُمّالِ بِإِضْرابٍ

sum: English uses except (for), but, with the exception of, bar; Arabic uses إِلّا, بِاسْتِثْناء, ما عَدا, غَيْر, سِوَى, each with its own case rule.
pts: After an affirmative, the noun after إِلّا is accusative; after a negative it takes its normal case.
After ما عَدا the noun is accusative; غَيْر and سِوَى head an iḍāfa; after بِاسْتِثْناء the noun is genitive.
ما عَدا and سِوَى follow a negative clause.
An English negative-plus-exception is often best translated with an affirmative and ‘only’.
ex: “Everyone came, except (for)/but a secretary.”
جاءَ كُلُّهُم إِلّا / ما عَدا السِّكْرِتِيرَةَ
“This is the best-selling product, bar none.”
إِنَّ هذا المُنْتَجَ أَكْثَرُ مَبِيعاً بِدُونِ اسْتِثْناءٍ
“I didn’t eat anything except the cheese.” (= I only ate the cheese)
ما أَكَلْتُ غَيْرَ جُبْنٍ / ما أَكَلْتُ شَيْئاً إِلّا جُبْناً

sum: English uses ‘What a …!’ and ‘such’. Arabic has several patterns.
pts: ما أَفْعَلَ + noun; حَبَّذا + nominative noun (with لَوْ + perfect: ‘how nice it would be if’); أَفْعِلْ بِـ + noun; كَفَى بِـ.
The frozen verbs بِئْسَ ‘how bad!’ and نِعْمَ ‘how good!’ take a nominative noun and do not inflect for gender.
ex: ‘What a wonderful book!’
ما أَجْمَلَ الكِتابَ
“How nice it would be if he did it!”
حَبَّذا (الحالُ) لَوْ عَمِلَهُ
“What a terrible man!”
بِئْسَ الرَّجُلُ

sum: All mean ‘not entirely’: ‘fairly’ is the weakest; ‘rather’ comes close to ‘very’; ‘pretty’ is informal and often means ‘very’; ‘quite’ can mean either ‘fairly’ or ‘fully’ (in US English ‘very’). Arabic uses إِلَى حَدٍّ ما / بِنَوْعٍ ما for ‘fairly’ and تَماماً for ‘fully’.
pts: Do not confuse ‘quite’ with ‘quiet’.
ex: “The results were fairly predictable.”
كانَتِ النَّتائِجُ مُتَوَقَّعَةً إِلَى حَدٍّ ما
“I am quite sure he is incompetent.”
أَنا مُتَأَكِّدٌ تَماماً أَنَّهُ غَيْرُ كُفْءٍ

sum: ‘Few’ and ‘fewer’ are for countables, ‘little’ and ‘less’ for uncountables. ‘A few’ and ‘a little’ are positive (some); ‘few’ and ‘little’ without ‘a’ are negative (not enough). ‘Lesser’ is formal and idiomatic. Arabic: قَلِيل (pl. قَلائِل), and أَقَلّ for less/fewer.
ex: “He is one of the few Arab thinkers who has a clearly defined philosophy.”
هُوَ واحِدٌ مِنَ المُفَكِّرِينَ العَرَبِ القَلائِلِ الَّذِينَ كانَتْ لَهُمْ فَلْسَفَةٌ مُحَدَّدَةٌ
“There was only little money left.”
ما بَقِيَ مِنَ المالِ إِلّا قَلِيلٌ
“He is the lesser of two evils!”
هُوَ أَقَلُّ الشَّرَّيْنِ / أَخَفُّ الضَّرَرَيْنِ

sum: Both mean ‘can catch fire’, but technical English uses only ‘flammable’, since ‘inflammable’ can be misread as ‘not flammable’; the negative is ‘non-flammable’. Arabic: قابِل لِلِاشْتِعال or قابِل لِلِالْتِهاب (قابِل لِلِاحْتِراق is ‘combustible’); non-flammable is غَيْرُ قابِلٍ لِلِاشْتِعال.
pts: ‘Inflammation’ (الْتِهاب) is medical only; ‘inflammatory’ outside medicine means inciting violence (تَحْرِيضِيّ).
ex: “Helium is non-flammable, as opposed to the dangerous hydrogen.”
إِنَّ غازَ الهِيلْيُوم غَيْرُ قابِلٍ لِلِاشْتِعالِ خِلافاً عَنِ الغازِ الهِيدْرُوجِين الخَطِيرِ
“Lebanese circles have strongly condemned the inflammatory media campaigns organized by militants from abroad.”
شَجَبَتِ الأَوْساطُ اللُّبْنانِيَّةُ الحَمَلاتِ الإِعْلامِيَّةَ التَّحْرِيضِيَّةَ الَّتي يُنَظِّمُها ناشِطُونَ مِنَ الخارِجِ

sum: The Arabic imperfect covers present and future: يَدْرُسُ الطّالِبُ can be ‘studies’ or ‘will study’. MSA marks the future with سَوْفَ or سَـ; careful writers use سَـ for the near future and سَوْفَ for the more distant or certain one. Context or a time adverb is often enough.
pts: English also uses ‘going to’ for planned actions.
Future perfect: سَيَكُونُ (قَدْ) + perfect; future progressive: سَيَكُونُ + participle; ‘future in the past’: كانَ سَـ + imperfect.
ex: “The vice-President will arrive tomorrow.”
يَصِلُ نائِبُ الرَّئِيسِ غَداً
“He will have been waiting for an hour before she arrives.”
سَيَكُونُ قَدِ انْتَظَرَ ساعَةً قَبْلَ وُصُولِها
“He would go on to win the nomination of the Republican party.”
كانَ سَيَفُوزُ بِتَرْشِيحِ الحِزْبِ الجُمْهُورِيِّ

sum: ‘Genial’ is cheerful (بَشُوش, باشّ, لَطِيف); a ‘genius’ is an extremely talented person or the talent itself (عَبْقَرِيّة); ‘ingenious’ is inventive (مُبْدِع, ماهِر, عَبْقَرِيّ); ‘ingenuous’ is innocent or naive (ساذَج).
ex: “His literary genius stood out in his first novel.”
بَرَزَتْ عَبْقَرِيَّتُهُ الأَدَبِيَّةُ في رِوايَتِهِ الأُولَى
“Either she is ingenuous/naïve or acting in collusion with him.”
هِيَ إِمّا ساذَجَةٌ أَوْ مُتَواطِئَةٌ مَعَهُ

sum: Arabic yes/no questions need هَلْ or أَ; English inverts verb and subject instead, so neither particle is translated. أَ is prefixed to the first word and cannot come before the article or a word starting with أ.
pts: In speech, and even formal discourse, the particle is often dropped; translators should not ‘classicize’ dialogue by adding it.
ex: “Will you approve the proposal?”
هَلْ تُوافِقُ عَلَى المُقْتَرَحِ؟
“This is the truth, isn’t it?”
هذِهِ هِيَ الحَقِيقَةُ أَلَيْسَ كَذلِكَ؟

sum: In careful usage, ‘take place’ (or ‘be held’) is for planned events; ‘happen’ and ‘occur’ for unexpected ones, so ‘the meeting happened yesterday’ is unidiomatic. Arabic: حَصَلَ for happen; أَجْرَى, قامَ, عَقَدَ, انْعَقَدَ, جَرَى for take place.
pts: ‘It occurred to me’: تَبادَرَ إِلَى ذِهْنِهِ, طَرَأَ عَلَى ذِهْنِهِ, خَطَرَ لَهُ / في بالِهِ, أُوحِيَ إِلَيْهِ, خُيِّلَ إِلَيْهِ, هَجَسَ في نَفْسِهِ.
ex: “I don’t understand what happened there.”
لا أَفْهَمُ ماذا حَصَلَ هُناكَ
“Last month the sessions of the sixty-fifth conference of the Cairo Academy of the Arabic Language took place.”
انْعَقَدَتِ الشَّهْرَ الماضِيَ جَلَساتُ مُؤْتَمَرِ الدَّوْرَةِ الخامِسَةِ وَالسِّتِّينَ لِمَجْمَعِ اللُّغَةِ العَرَبِيَّةِ في القاهِرَةِ
“It occurred to me that I should respond to his accusations.”
خُيِّلَ إِلَيَّ أَنَّ مِنَ الضَّرُورِيِّ أَنْ أُجِيبَ عَلَى اتِّهاماتِهِ

sum: ‘Hardly’, ‘scarcely’ and ‘barely’ mean almost not, or with difficulty: ما كادَ, لا يَكادُ, لَمْ يَمْضِ, قَلَّما. They are already negative, so English needs no second negative (‘scarcely any’, not ‘scarcely no’).
pts: For ‘immediately after’, they are followed by ‘when’; ‘no sooner’ means the same but takes ‘than’. Arabic: ما كادَ / لا يَكادُ / لَمْ يَكَدْ … حَتَّى; ما إِنْ … حَتَّى; لَمْ يَمْضِ … حَتَّى.
ex: “Barely a day went by without insults and humiliations.”
ما كادَ يَمُرُّ يَوْمٌ واحِدٌ دُونَ شَتائِمَ وَإِهاناتٍ
“No sooner did the president read this report than he ordered that the situation be improved.”
ما إِنْ قَرَأَ الرَّئِيسُ هذا التَّقْرِيرَ حَتَّى أَمَرَ بِتَصْحِيحِ الوَضْعِ

sum: ‘High’ is the opposite of ‘low’ (distance from the ground) and is used for things; ‘tall’ is the opposite of ‘short’, meaning higher than average, for people and for high narrow things. Arabic uses طَوِيل for ‘tall’ and ‘long’ alike (رَجُلٌ طَوِيلٌ, شُعُورٌ طَوِيلَةٌ), so take care, and عالٍ for height (جَبَلٌ عالٍ).
ex: “We climbed a high mountain.”
قَدْ تَسَلَّقْنا جَبَلاً عالِياً
“Can you see that tall building over there?”
هَلْ تُشاهِدُ ذلِكَ المَبْنَى العالِيَ؟

sum: All are about buying or selling the right to use something. In British English ‘hire’ is short-term and ‘rent’ longer (US: ‘rent’ for both); add ‘out’ to stress selling the use. ‘Let’ is only for buildings (British), ‘charter’ for ships and planes, ‘lease’ for buildings or vehicles (and ‘a lease’ is the contract). Arabic makes no time distinction: أَجَّرَ, اسْتَأْجَرَ, كارَى, أَكْرَى, اكْتَرَى, اسْتَكْرَى; ‘rent’ is أُجْرة, إِيجار, كِراء.
pts: ‘For rent/hire’ and ‘to let’: لِلْإِيجار.
ex: “He rented a flat with only two rooms.”
اسْتَأْجَرَ شَقَّةً صَغِيرَةً تَتَكَوَّنُ مِنْ غُرْفَتَيْنِ فَقَطْ
“They rented out their land to the farmers.”
أَجَّرُوا أَراضِيَهُمْ لِلْمُزارِعِينَ
“The government delegation chartered a private plane for their European tour.”
اسْتَأْجَرَ الوَفْدُ الحُكُومِيُّ طائِرَةً خاصَّةً لِجَوْلَتِهِ الأُورُوبِيَّةِ

sum: ‘Historic’ is of great significance; ‘historical’ relates to (the study of) history. Both tend to be تارِيخِيّ in Arabic.
ex: “This theory generally leads to the concealment of the historical dimension of the text.”
تُفْضِي هذِهِ النَّظَرِيَّةُ غالِباً إِلَى إِخْفاءِ البُعْدِ التّارِيخِيِّ لِلنَّصِّ
“They were inflicted a historic defeat during the world championships.”
تَكَبَّدُوا هَزِيمَةً تارِيخِيَّةً في بُطُولَةِ العالَمِ

sum: ‘Holiday’ is the general word (go ‘on holiday’, not ‘holidays’); ‘public holidays’ are set by law; a ‘day off’ is not an ‘off day’. ‘Vacation’ is the long university break (US: any holiday); ‘leave’ is for soldiers, and for ‘maternity’ or ‘sick leave’; courts and parliament have a ‘recess’.
pts: Arabic uses عُطْلة or إِجازة for everything; careful writers avoid إِجازة, felt to be Egyptian and also meaning a degree or an authorization.
‘Vacant’ and ‘vacancy’ (empty, unfilled) are شاغِر (pl. شَواغِر) or خالٍ.
ex: “His Highness the Emir attended the celebrations on the occasion of the Kuwaiti National Day.”
حَضَرَ صاحِبُ السُّمُوِّ الأَمِيرُ الاحْتِفالاتِ بِمُناسَبَةِ العُطْلَةِ الوَطَنِيَّةِ لِدَوْلَةِ الكُوَيْتِ
“The court recess runs every year from the first of July until the end of September.”
تَبْدَأُ العُطْلَةُ القَضائِيَّةُ كُلَّ عامٍ مِنْ أَوَّلِ يُولْيُو وَتَنْتَهِي آخِرَ سِبْتَمْبِر
“Are there any vacancies/vacant positions in the company now?”
هَلْ هُناكَ وَظائِفُ شاغِرَةٌ / خالِيَةٌ في الشَّرِكَةِ الآنَ؟

sum: ‘Human’ is about people and mankind; ‘humane’ is compassionate and is related to ‘humanitarian’. Arabic uses إِنْسانِيّ for all of them.
ex: “Islamic slaughter is not considered humane under French law.”
يَعْتَبِرُ القانُونُ الفَرَنْسِيُّ الذَّبْحَ عَلَى الطَّرِيقَةِ الإِسْلامِيَّةِ غَيْرَ إِنْسانِيٍّ
“… crimes against humanity.”
جَرائِمُ ضِدَّ الإِنْسانِيَّةِ

sum: English hyphenates compound adjectives before a noun to show they act as one unit (a well-known author, blue-green eyes, a four-week holiday, with no plural -s), and to mean ‘from … to’ (Arabic-English translation). Arabic traditionally has no hyphens and spells these out, often in a single word.
pts: The one exception where Arabic follows English, التَّرْجَمَةُ إِنْكِلِيزِيّ-عَرَبِيّ, is felt to be non-standard; التَّرْجَمَةُ مِنَ الإِنْكِلِيزِيِّ إِلَى العَرَبِيِّ is preferred.
ex: ‘high-frequency sound waves’
أَمْواجٌ صَوْتِيَّةٌ عالِيَةُ التَّرَدُّدِ
‘four-week holiday’
عُطْلَةٌ لِأَرْبَعَةِ أَسابِيعَ
‘blue-green eyes’
عُيُونٌ خُضْرٌ زُرْقٌ

sum: In reported yes/no questions ‘if’ and ‘whether’ are often interchangeable; Arabic uses إِذا / إِنْ, أَ … أَمْ for alternatives, or a prepositional phrase. Only ‘whether’ works before ‘to + infinitive’, after a preposition, at the start of a sentence, and with ‘or not’.
ex: “Do you know if/whether he’ll be at home or at work?”
هَلْ تَعْرِفُ إِنْ / إِذا كانَ في البَيْتِ أَمْ في المَكْتَبِ؟
“Everything depends on whether they will be able to sell the house.”
كُلُّ شَيْءٍ يَعْتَمِدُ عَلَى تَمَكُّنِهِمْ مِنْ بَيْعِ البَيْتِ
“It doesn’t matter whether or not he chooses to resign.”
لا يُهِمُّ إِذا / إِنْ قَرَّرَ أَنْ يَسْتَقِيلَ (أَمْ لا)

sum: ‘In case’ allows for a possibility; ‘in case of’ means ‘in the event of’; ‘in no case’ means under no circumstances. Arabic renders these with حال (في حالَةِ, في أَيِّ حالٍ). ‘In spite of’ (= despite) uses رَغْم.
ex: “The detention can in no case be more than three days.”
لا يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يَزِيدَ التَّوْقِيفُ في أَيِّ حالٍ عَلَى ثَلاثَةِ أَيّامٍ
“In case of rain, you can collect water.”
تَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ تَجْمَعَ المِياهَ في حالَةِ سُقُوطِ المَطَرِ
“The population made preparations for Ramadan despite the blockade.”
بِرَغْمِ الحِصارِ اسْتَعَدَّ الشَّعْبُ لِشَهْرِ رَمَضانَ

sum: ‘Incredible’ is hard to believe (لا يُصَدَّق); ‘incredulous’ shows disbelief (مُرْتاب). ‘Credulous’ is naive or gullible.
ex: “He told me an incredible story about how he was attacked by sharks.”
لَقَدْ حَكَى لي قِصَّةً لا تُصَدَّقُ عَنْ كَيْفِيَّةِ مُهاجَمَةِ أَسْماكِ القِرْشِ لَهُ
“They looked at her with an incredulous expression on their faces.”
لَقَدْ نَظَرُوا إِلَيْها وَعَلَى وُجُوهِهِمْ نَظْرَةٌ مُرْتابَةٌ

sum: ‘Industrial’ relates to industry (صِناعِيّ); ‘industrious’ is hardworking (مُجْتَهِد).
ex: “If a pupil is industrious, he will get the secondary school certificate.”
وَإِذا كانَ التِّلْمِيذُ مُجْتَهِداً فَسَيَحْصُلُ عَلَى شَهادَةِ الثّانَوِيَّةِ العامَّةِ

sum: ‘Information’ is uncountable in English (no ‘informations’), but Arabic usually uses a plural: أَخْبار, مَعْلُومات, اسْتِعْلامات. ‘Minister for Information’ is وَزِيرُ الإِعْلامِ.
ex: “The information desk is on the second floor.”
يَقَعُ مَكْتَبُ الاسْتِعْلاماتِ في الطّابِقِ الثّانِي
“We have no information regarding foreign fighters on the outskirts of the city.”
لَيْسَتْ لَدَيْنا أَيُّ مَعْلُوماتٍ عَنْ وُجُودِ مُقاتِلِينَ أَجانِبَ عَلَى مَشارِفِ المَدِينَةِ

sum: ‘Interrupt’ stops someone briefly (قَطَعَ, انْقَطَعَ); ‘intervene’ steps in to find a solution or mediate (داخَلَ, تَوَسَّطَ); ‘interfere’ is unwanted intervention (تَدَخَّلَ).
ex: “The Organization of the Islamic Conference (OIC) will intervene between the two parties.”
سَتَتَوَسَّطُ مُنَظَّمَةُ المُؤْتَمَرِ الإِسْلامِيِّ بَيْنَ الطَّرَفَيْنِ
“The main thing is that the state should not interfere in economic activity.”
أَهَمُّ شَيْءٍ هُوَ أَلّا تَتَدَخَّلَ الدَّوْلَةُ في النَّشاطِ الاقْتِصادِيِّ

sum: ‘Intolerable’ cannot be tolerated (informally, irritating): لا يُطاق, غَيْرُ مُحْتَمَل. ‘Intolerant’ lacks respect for others and their beliefs: غَيْرُ مُتَسامِح, sometimes مُتَعَصِّب (fanatical).
ex: “They responded to the intolerable provocation in an appropriate and lawful manner.”
رَدُّوا عَلَى الاسْتِفْزازِ الَّذِي لا يُطاقُ بِطَرِيقَةٍ مُناسِبَةٍ وَمَشْرُوعَةٍ
“This view is part of an intolerant colonialist mindset.”
تَنْدَرِجُ هذِهِ الرُّؤْيَةُ في إِطارِ عَقْلِيَّةٍ اسْتِعْمارِيَّةٍ مُتَعَصِّبَةٍ

sum: Despite the prefix, ‘invaluable’ means too precious to price (لا يُقَدَّرُ بِثَمَن, لا يُثَمَّن); ‘valueless’ is worthless (بِلا / بِدُونِ قِيمَة).
ex: “This painting is invaluable.”
لا تُقَدَّرُ هذِهِ اللَّوْحَةُ بِثَمَنٍ
“Counterfeit money is valueless.”
الأَمْوالُ المُزَيَّفَةُ بِلا قِيمَةٍ

sum: ‘Judicial’ relates to the courts (قَضائِيّ); ‘judicious’ is prudent (حَكِيم, حَصِيف); ‘judiciary’ and ‘judicature’ are the body of judges (جَماعَةُ القُضاة).
ex: “The Central Bank imposed a judicious loans policy.”
فَرَضَ البَنْكُ المَرْكَزِيُّ سِياسَةَ إِقْراضٍ حَصِيفَةً
“The union expressed the view of the judiciary on the ongoing struggle …”
أَفْصَحَتِ النِّقابَةُ عَنْ رَأْيِ (جَماعَةِ) القُضاةِ في مِصْرَ …

sum: As a time adverb, ‘just’ goes with a perfect tense; ‘just now’ means a moment ago or at this moment. Arabic: لِتَوِّ + pronoun with the perfect. ‘Just’ meaning ‘only’ is فَقَطْ.
ex: “We have just finished eating.”
لَقَدِ انْتَهَيْنا لِتَوِّنا مِنْ تَناوُلِ الطَّعامِ
“I’m just saying that you shouldn’t shout at her like that.”
أَنا أَقُولُ فَقَطْ أَنَّهُ لا يَنْبَغِي أَنْ تَصْرُخِي في وَجْهِها هكَذا

sum: This progressive construction is rendered by ‘sisters of كانَ’ such as ظَلَّ and ما زالَ / لا يَزالُ with the imperfect. Despite its past form, ما زالَ is translated with an English present.
ex: “He keeps on writing and his pen does not stop detailing stories and novels on paper.”
يَظَلُّ يَكْتُبُ وَلا يَتَوَقَّفُ قَلَمُهُ عَنْ سَرْدِ الحِكاياتِ وَالرِّواياتِ عَلَى الوَرَقِ
“She keeps on talking about the party’s desire to win the local elections.”
لا تَزالُ تَتَحَدَّثُ عَنْ رَغْبَةِ الحِزْبِ في الفَوْزِ في الانْتِخاباتِ المَحَلِّيَّةِ

sum: In American English ‘lawyer’, ‘attorney’ and ‘counselor’ are interchangeable; in England ‘lawyer’ is general while ‘solicitor’ and ‘barrister’ are specific kinds; ‘advocate’ is used in some systems such as Scotland’s. Arabic has one word, مُحامٍ, so the generic ‘lawyer’ is usually the right translation.
ex: “The two lawyers brought a case before the Administrative Tribunal of Mansoura.”
أَقامَ المُحامِيانِ دَعْوَى أَمامَ مَحْكَمَةِ القَضاءِ الإِدارِيِّ بِالمَنْصُورَةِ

sum: The hortative ‘let’s’ takes an infinitive in English. Arabic uses the imperative lām (لِـ, or فَلْـ) with the jussive, the interjection هَيّا (often with بِـ before a pronoun), or دَعْ with a suffix.
ex: “Let’s go.”
لِنَذْهَبْ / فَلْنَذْهَبْ / دَعْنا نَذْهَبْ
“Let’s study French!”
هَيّا بِنا نَتَعَلَّمُ الفَرَنْسِيَّةَ

sum: Both are often عَمِلَ or فَعَلَ in Arabic, interchangeably. When ‘make’ is causative (make someone do something), Arabic uses جَعَلَ as an auxiliary.
ex: “I did my homework.”
عَمِلْتُ / فَعَلْتُ وَظائِفِي
“These jokes will make you laugh.”
سَتَجْعَلُكَ هذِهِ النُّكَتُ تَضْحَكُ
“He made me the laughing-stock of the entire university.”
جَعَلَنِي أُضْحُوكَةَ الجامِعَةِ كُلِّها

sum: All link to the sea but have their own collocates: ‘maritime’ for shipping and navigation, ‘nautical’ for maps and speeds (nautical mile), ‘naval’ for the Navy, ‘marine’ for sea life. Arabic uses بَحْرِيّ for all (مِلاحِيّ for navigation), so the difficulty is mostly Arabic into English.
pts: ‘Navy’ is capitalized for the military; ‘merchant navy’ is أُسْطُولٌ تِجارِيٌّ.
ex: “The new maritime trade law will come into force next month.”
يَدْخُلُ القانُونُ الجَدِيدُ لِلتِّجارَةِ البَحْرِيَّةِ حَيِّزَ التَّنْفِيذِ الشَّهْرَ القادِمَ
“Fishermen are afraid of the depletion of marine wildlife.”
يَتَخَوَّفُ الصَّيّادُونَ مِنِ اسْتِنْزافِ الثَّرْوَةِ الحَيَوانِيَّةِ البَحْرِيَّةِ

sum: ‘Maybe’ is an adverb (perhaps): رُبَّما, لَعَلَّ, يُمْكِنُ / مُمْكِنٌ أَنْ. ‘May be’ is a verb phrase: it is possible that.
ex: “Maybe most of the articles in the new law are controversial.”
لَعَلَّ أَكْثَرَ مَوادِّ القانُونِ الجَدِيدِ مُثِيرَةٌ لِلْجَدَلِ
“It may be difficult to forgive him, but he is your father.”
يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يَكُونَ غُفْرانُ مُعامَلَتِهِ صَعْباً عَلَيْكَ وَلكِنَّهُ أَبُوكَ

sum: ‘Moral’ is a noun (an ethical rule) or adjective (ethical): خُلُق, pl. أَخْلاق, adj. خُلُقِيّ, أَخْلاقِيّ. ‘Morale’ is only a noun, mental confidence: رُوحٌ مَعْنَوِيَّةٌ.
ex: “This principle has no moral/ethical basis.”
لَيْسَ لِهذا المَبْدَإِ أُسُسٌ أَخْلاقِيَّةٌ
“The victory will urge the players to enter the championships with heightened morale.”
الفَوْزُ يَدْفَعُ اللّاعِبِينَ إِلَى دُخُولِ البُطُولاتِ بِرُوحٍ مَعْنَوِيَّةٍ عالِيَةٍ

sum: ‘Most’ can mean ‘very’; ‘mostly’ means ‘particularly’. In comparisons ‘more’ is for two and ‘most’ for three or more; Arabic makes no such distinction and uses a superlative for both.
ex: “I was most (= very) impressed by his performance.”
أَعْجَبَنِي أَداؤُهُ جِدّاً
“I was mostly (= particularly) impressed by his performance.”
أَعْجَبَنِي أَداؤُهُ بِصِفَةٍ خاصَّةٍ
“This is the more complex solution of the two.”
هذا هُوَ أَكْثَرُ الحَلَّيْنِ تَعْقِيداً

sum: ‘Many’ is for countables, ‘much’ for uncountables (like ‘a great deal’); Arabic uses كَثِير for both, and for adverbial ‘much’. ‘Many a’ + singular noun is a formal ‘many’.
ex: “The government did not achieve much.”
لَمْ تُحَقِّقِ الحُكُومَةُ كَثِيراً
“Many a student fell into this trap.”
وَقَعَ كَثِيرٌ مِنَ الطُّلّابِ في هذِهِ المَصْيَدَةِ

sum: ‘Nevertheless’ (= nonetheless) means ‘in spite of that’: مَعَ أَنَّ, عَلَى الرَّغْمِ مِنْ ذلِكَ, بِالرَّغْمِ مِنْ ذلِكَ, رَغْمَ, بِرَغْمِ. Do not confuse it with ‘none the less’ (not less). ‘Notwithstanding’ is formal or legal and often follows its object.
ex: “Nevertheless, we shall be forced to go ahead with the plans.”
بِالرَّغْمِ مِنْ ذلِكَ فَإِنَّنا سَنُضْطَرُّ إِلَى تَنْفِيذِ الخُطَطِ
“She travelled to Egypt, doctor’s orders notwithstanding.”
سافَرَتْ إِلَى مِصْرَ بِرَغْمِ نَصِيحَةِ طَبِيبِها

sum: English always puts north/south before east/west; Arabic allows either an iḍāfa or a noun with a nisba adjective (شَمال شَرْق / شَمال شَرْقِيّ).
pts: Capitals mark a defined geopolitical entity: ‘North-South dialogue’ (حِوارُ شَمالٍ جَنُوبٍ), ‘North Africa’ (الشَّمالِيَّةُ إِفْرِيقْيا), which excludes Egypt.
The ‘-ern’ forms are undefined areas, not capitalized: ‘South Africa’ (إِفْرِيقْيا الجَنُوبِيَّة) versus ‘southern Africa’ (جَنُوبُ إِفْرِيقْيا).
‘East of the capital’: شَرْقَ العاصِمَةِ.
ex: “The troops moved towards the southeast (NOT *eastsouth) of the country.”
زَحَفَ الجَيْشُ إِلَى جَنُوبِ شَرْقِ البِلادِ
“The region east of the capital was hit by the storm.”
كانَتِ المِنْطَقَةُ شَرْقَ العاصِمَةِ مُصابَةً بِالعاصِفَةِ

ar: ما لبث أن / لم يمضِ … حتى
sum: ‘It was not long before’ and ‘it didn’t take long before’ are rendered with لَبِثَ and مَضَى: ما لَبِثَ / لَمْ يَلْبَثْ + أَنْ / حَتَّى + perfect; لا يَلْبَثُ / لَنْ يَلْبَثَ + حَتَّى / أَنْ + subjunctive; لَمْ يَمْضِ / لَنْ يَمْضِيَ + حَتَّى.
ex: “It wasn’t long before the militia responded to the attack on its headquarters.”
ما لَبِثَتْ أَنْ رَدَّتِ الكَتائِبُ عَلَى اقْتِحامِ مَقَرِّها
“It wasn’t long before she discovered that he had not warned them of the danger.”
لَمْ تَلْبَثْ أَنِ اكْتَشَفَتْ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يُحَذِّرْهُمْ مِنَ الخَطَرِ

sum: Arabic builds this with a negative (لَمْ + jussive, لا + imperfect, لَنْ + subjunctive, or لَيْسَ + nominal sentence), then فَحَسْبُ / فَقَطْ, then بَلْ …, and often أَيْضاً or كَذلِكَ at the end.
ex: “He was not only a university teacher and educationalist but also a critic and a writer.”
لَمْ يَكُنْ أُسْتاذاً جامِعِيّاً وَمُرَبِّياً فَقَطْ بَلْ ناقِداً وَكاتِباً كَذلِكَ
“It is not just a mistake ethically, but also – and above all else – unproductive.”
لَيْسَتْ خاطِئَةً أَخْلاقِيّاً فَحَسْبُ بَلْ هِيَ، قَبْلَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ، غَيْرُ مُثْمِرَةٍ

sum: Like ‘let alone’ or ‘to say nothing of’: ناهِيكَ عَنْ / مِنْ, بِغَضِّ النَّظَرِ عَنْ, فَضْلاً عَنْ (in media Arabic sometimes فَضْلاً عَنْ أَنَّ). فَضْلاً عَنْ ذلِكَ can also mean ‘besides, furthermore’.
ex: “The Ministry cannot pay the pensioners, not to mention/let alone the unemployed.”
لا تَسْتَطِيعُ الوِزارَةُ أَنْ تَدْفَعَ لِلْمُتَقاعِدِينَ ناهِيكَ / فَضْلاً عَنِ العاطِلِينَ
“Besides, he acquired significant in-depth expertise in this field.”
فَضْلاً عَنْ ذلِكَ فَإِنَّهُ اكْتَسَبَ خِبْرَةً واسِعَةً وَعَمِيقَةً في هذا المَجالِ

sum: ‘Number’ is a quantity or the symbol for it; ‘digit’, ‘figure’ and ‘numeral’ are the symbol. Arabic: عَدَد (pl. أَعْداد) for quantities and series, رَقْم (pl. أَرْقام) for the figure.
pts: عَدَد for a newspaper or magazine is ‘issue’.
‘A number of’ (several) is عَدَدٌ مِنْ (never with the article) or عِدَّة in apposition, with a plural verb in English; ‘the number of’ is an iḍāfa with عَدَد.
ex: “You have to write the numbers in digits.”
يَجِبُ أَنْ تَكْتُبَ الأَعْدادَ بِأَرْقامٍ
“The article … was published in the eighth issue of the journal.”
نُشِرَتِ المَقالَةُ … في العَدَدِ الثّامِنِ لِلْمَجَلَّةِ
“The police arrested a number of/several thieves.”
قَبَضَتِ الشُّرْطَةُ عَلَى لُصُوصٍ عِدَّةٍ / عَدَدٍ مِنَ اللُّصُوصِ

sum: English grades obligation from strong (must, have to) to medium (should) to weak (ought to); ‘must’ is internal (the speaker’s own) and ‘have to’ external. Arabic has a parallel set of verbs, prepositions and adverbial phrases.
pts: Strong: يَجِبُ (عَلَى), يَتَحَتَّمُ عَلَى, يَتَعَيَّنُ عَلَى (incumbent), يَتَوَجَّبُ عَلَى, مِنَ الواجِبِ عَلَى, مِنَ اللّازِمِ, لا مَنْدُوحَةَ عَنْ (imperative), لا بُدَّ مِنْ / لا مَفَرَّ مِنْ (inescapable), لا مَناصَ مِنْهُ (unavoidable).
Advisability, descending: مِنَ الضَّرُورِيِّ أَنْ, يَنْبَغِي أَنْ, يُسْتَحْسَنُ أَنْ, يَجْدُرُ (بِهِ) + verbal noun; weak: مِنَ الأَحْسَنِ.
‘Had better’ (often threatening): يَتَعَيَّنُ. ‘Be supposed to’: يُفْتَرَضُ أَنْ, مِنَ المُفْتَرَضِ أَنْ.
‘Should have’ + participle: كانَ يَنْبَغِي أَنْ (past expectation), كانَ مِنَ الواجِبِ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ (past obligation).
‘Mustn’t’ is يَجِبُ أَلّا; ‘needn’t’ is لا يَجِبُ أَنْ, لَيْسَ لِزاماً, لَيْسَ مُلْزَماً, لا حاجَةَ أَنْ; ‘must be / must have been’ (near certainty) is لا بُدَّ أَنَّ (+ قَدْ كانَ).
ex: “The curricula have to be designed with the children’s ages in mind.”
يَجِبُ أَنْ تُوضَعَ المَناهِجُ الدِّراسِيَّةُ مَعَ مُراعاةِ عُمْرِ الأَطْفالِ
“Every journalist has to/must follow his conscience.”
يَتَوَجَّبُ عَلَى كُلِّ صُحُفِيٍّ أَنْ يَتَّبِعَ ضَمِيرَهُ
“The committee should widen its scope.”
يُسْتَحْسَنُ أَنْ تُوَسِّعَ اللَّجْنَةُ عَمَلَها
“The Supreme Court is supposed to hand down its decision in mid-June.”
مِنَ المُفْتَرَضِ أَنْ تُصْدِرَ المَحْكَمَةُ العُلْيا قَرارَها في مُنْتَصَفِ حَزِيران (يُونْيُو)
“We needn’t attend the next meeting.”
لا حاجَةَ أَنْ نَحْضُرَ الاجْتِماعَ المُقْبِلَ
“The teacher must have been in his office.”
لا بُدَّ أَنَّ الأُسْتاذَ قَدْ كانَ في مَكْتَبِهِ في هذا الوَقْتِ

sum: English builds the passive with an auxiliary and a past participle. Arabic has more options, and normally does not name the agent.
pts: 1. Inflection: most verb forms have a passive (not VII and IX; V and VI rarely).
2. Form I verbs with inherent passive meaning.
3. Derived forms with passive or middle meaning (V, VII, VIII, IX): تَفَرَّقَ, انْفَعَلَ, اِحْمَرَّ.
4. The periphrastic passive with تَمَّ or جَرَى + verbal noun, popular in media Arabic.
The agent is not stated in standard Arabic, except instruments with بِـ; media Arabic uses مِنْ طَرَفِ, عَلَى يَدِ, مِنْ قِبَلِ, which careful writers frown on.
Ditransitive verbs keep the second object in the accusative (أُعْطِيَ الجِنِرالُ هَدِيَّةً); with indirect transitive verbs the verb stays masculine singular (حُكِمَ عَلَى المُجْرِمِينَ).

Some Arabic passives are English actives (تُوُفِّيَ ‘he died’), and many carry potential meaning, best rendered with ‘-able/-ible’: مَسْمُوع ‘audible’, لا يُطاق ‘unbearable’, لا يُنْسَى ‘unforgettable’, لا يُعَدّ ‘countless’, لا يُدْحَض ‘irrefutable’.
ex: “Several guards were killed near the presidential palace.”
قُتِلَ بَعْضُ الحُرّاسِ قُرْبَ قَصْرِ الرِّئاسَةِ
“The agreement was concluded in Tunis.”
أُبْرِمَتِ الاتِّفاقِيَّةُ في تُونِس
“The goals of this strategy are being investigated.”
يَتِمُّ تَحْقِيقُ أَهْدافِ هذِهِ الاسْتِراتِيجِيّاتِ
“The letter was written with invisible ink.”
كُتِبَتِ الرِّسالَةُ بِحِبْرٍ لا مَرْئِيٍّ

sum: Arabic expresses the past mainly with the perfect (with or without كانَ); English has six past tenses: simple past, present perfect, past perfect, and their progressive forms. Mapping them takes care.
pts: Present perfect (progressive): the imperfect with مُنْذُ and a time adverbial, or ما زالَ / لا يَزالُ / لَمْ يَزَلْ; مُنْذُ in a nominal sentence also gives a present perfect.
كانَ يَفْعَلُ is ‘used to’; كانَ + active participle is a past progressive; the past progressive often marks simultaneity.

Some Arabic perfects are English presents: states (تَعِبَ ‘he is tired’, عَطِشَ, جاعَ), decisions and agreement (اتَّفَقْنا ‘we are in agreement’), and wishes (بارَكَ اللهُ فِيكَ ‘(May) God bless you’).
Past perfect can be (قَدْ) سَبَقَ أَنْ + perfect.
قَدْ and لَقَدْ mark near past or completion: ‘(only) fifteen minutes ago’, ‘indeed’.
ex: “He has been a revolutionary for forty years.”
لَمْ يَزَلْ ثائِراً مُنْذُ أَرْبَعِينَ عاماً
“During his university days, he used to write comedies.”
كانَ يَكْتُبُ المَسْرَحِيّاتِ الكُومِيدِيَّةَ في أَثْناءِ دِراسَتِهِ بِالجامِعَةِ
“We had put forward the principal goals of the strategy in the previous article.”
سَبَقَ أَنْ عَرَضْنا الأَهْدافَ الرَّئِيسِيَّةَ لِلِاسْتِراتِيجِيَّةِ في المَقالِ السّابِقِ
“The new law indeed came into effect yesterday.”
قَدْ دَخَلَ القانُونُ الجَدِيدُ في حَيِّزِ التَّنْفِيذِ أَمْسِ

sum: Prefixes are mainly an English-into-Arabic problem: Arabic affixes are few and grammatical, while many English prefixes are Latin or Greek and sometimes no longer felt as prefixes at all (diagnosis, تَشْخِيص). Translate the meaning, not the morpheme, and check whether the ‘prefix’ is really part of the root (epistle, رِسالة) or a true one (epicentre).
pts: Methods: a simple word (‘recreate’, جَدَّدَ); an iḍāfa (‘overproduction’, إِفْراطُ الإِنْتاجِ); a prepositional phrase (‘subterranean’, تَحْتَ سَطْحِ الأَرْضِ; ‘supernatural’, فَوْقَ الطَّبِيعَةِ); a noun phrase (‘low-born’, وَضِيعُ النَّسَبِ); a compound (‘decentralization’, لامَرْكَزِيَّة); noun + preposition + noun (‘subspecies’, فَرْعٌ مِنَ الفَرْعِ).
Arabic dislikes compounding, so it prefers an iḍāfa; recent coinings with a clearly meaningful prefix are the likeliest to get a separate word.
Several English prefixes share one Arabic word: contra-, counter-, anti- tend to be مُضادّ (rather than ضِدّ).
Spelling in English: the more established the word, the more likely it is written solid; a hyphen separates vowel clashes (pre-eminence) and always precedes a proper noun (trans-Siberian).
