sum: The English simple present (states, general truths, stative verbs, habits) is usually the Arabic imperfect, or a nominal sentence for ‘to be’. The present progressive (happening now, or temporary; never with stative verbs) is the imperfect, an active participle with intransitive verbs, or قامَ بِـ + verbal noun.
pts: Both presents can refer to the near future: سَـ / سَوْفَ + imperfect.
The imperfect is negated with لا; a participle with لَيْسَ.
‘Have’ for possession or illness is not progressive: ‘I have a headache’ (عِنْدِي صُداعٌ), not *‘I am having a headache’.
ex: “The sun sets in the west.”
تَأْفُلُ الشَّمْسُ في المَغْرِبِ
“I am coming/on my way.”
أَنا قادِمٌ
“The opposition are organizing unprecedented demonstrations against the government.”
تَقُومُ المُعارَضَةُ بِاحْتِجاجاتٍ غَيْرِ مَسْبُوقَةٍ ضِدَّ الحُكُومَةِ
“I am not travelling today.”
لَسْتُ مُسافِراً اليَوْمَ

sum: ‘Presently’ means in a short while: عَنْ / بَعْدَ قَلِيلٍ, عَمّا / عَنْ / مِنْ قَرِيبٍ with the imperfect, with or without سَـ / سَوْفَ. ‘At present’ means now: في الوَقْتِ الحاضِرِ, الآنَ.
ex: “We will have a solution presently.”
سَيَكُونُ لَدَيْنا حَلٌّ عَمّا قَرِيبٍ
“She is leaving at present.”
تُغادِرُ الآنَ

sum: A ‘price’ is what you pay (سِعْر, pl. أَسْعار; ثَمَن, pl. أَثْمان); a ‘prize’ is what you win (جائِزَة, pl. جَوائِز). ‘Price’ goes with ‘pay’ (دَفَعَ) and, in Arabic, with ‘cost’ (كَلَّفَ); ‘prize’ with ‘award’ (مَنَحَ), ‘win’ (أَحْرَزَ, حازَ, فازَ) and ‘receive’ (تَسَلَّمَ).
pts: On the stock exchange, سِعْر is preferred to ثَمَن.
ex: “He won/received the Nobel Prize for chemistry.”
أَحْرَزَ / تَسَلَّمَ / حازَ عَلَى / فازَ بِجائِزَةِ نُوبِل في الكِيمِياءِ
“No matter how much it cost.”
مَهْما كَلَّفَ الثَّمَنُ
“Share prices have continued to rise at the stock exchange.”
اسْتَمَرَّتْ أَسْعارُ الأَسْهُمِ في الارْتِفاعِ في البُورْصَةِ

sum: ‘Principal’ as a noun is the head of a school or college (مُدِير); as an adjective it means chief (رَئِيسِيّ). ‘Principle’ is only a noun, a basis for beliefs or actions (مَبْدَأ, pl. مَبادِئ).
ex: “The principal opposition parties decided on a plan to put forward two joint nominees.”
أَقَرَّتِ الأَحْزابُ الرَّئِيسِيَّةُ في المُعارَضَةِ خُطَّةً لِتَقْدِيمِ مُرَشَّحَيْنِ مُشْتَرَكَيْنِ
“There was an agreement on the principle of withdrawal.”
كانَ هُناكَ اتِّفاقٌ حَوْلَ مَبْدَإِ الانْسِحابِ

sum: English punctuation is tightly ruled; Arabic punctuation is a 20th-century borrowing from Western (mostly English) practice and is used very inconsistently, so the translator has to normalize it.
pts: Quotation marks (عَلاماتُ اقْتِباس): Arabic also uses them for emphasis, foreign company names and dialect words, where English uses italics or nothing; forms range from «…» to “…”.

Round brackets (قَوْسانِ): still used for Qur’anic quotation (hence بَيْنَ القَوْسَيْنِ, ‘in inverted commas’), and in formal Arabic for foreign names, borrowings, titles, foreign abbreviations and asides. In English: omit for names, titles and abbreviations; italics for borrowings; keep for asides.
Exclamation and question marks: Arabic piles them up for intensity (!؟); English uses one.

Suspension points (…): English uses them only in literature, for a pause or unfinished thought, never for ‘etc.’; Arabic uses them freely at the end of lists or for emphasis, so they are usually dropped or replaced by a comma.
ex: According to the CEO of Exxon Mobil the price of oil will have to be between 60 and 70 dollars per barrel.
قالَ رَئِيسُ شَرِكَةِ «إِكْسُون مُوبِيل»: يَجِبُ أَنْ يَتَراوَحَ سِعْرُ بَرْمِيلِ النَّفْطِ بَيْنَ 60 وَ70 دُولاراً
“We spoke with the actress during the shooting of the soap Nur Maryam.”
تَحَدَّثْنا مَعَ الفَنّانَةِ في كَوالِيسِ مُسَلْسَلِ (نُور مَرْيَم)
“Who is responsible, the police or the demonstrators?”
مَنِ المَسْؤُولُ: الشُّرْطَةُ أَمِ المُتَظاهِرُونَ؟!

sum: English chooses who/whom/which/that/whose/where by person, place or thing, by grammatical role, and by preposition, and separates defining clauses (no commas, pronoun can drop) from non-defining ones (with commas). Arabic ignores human versus non-human; what matters is whether the antecedent is definite. Only definite antecedents take a relative pronoun.
pts: Forms: الَّذِي, الَّتِي; dual اللَّذانِ / اللَّذَيْنِ, اللَّتانِ / اللَّتَيْنِ; plural الَّذِينَ, اللّاتِي / اللَّواتِي.
Arabic needs a resumptive pronoun (عائِد) when the antecedent is the object of a verb or preposition; this is why Arabic speakers write *‘the house that I lived in it’.
Place: ‘where’ (حَيْثُ, with a fixed ending).
Indefinite antecedent: no pronoun: رَجُلٌ كانَ هُناكَ ‘a man who was there’.
Non-specific: whichever (أَيّ), whatsoever (أَيّ, ما, ماذا, مَهْما), whoever (مَنْ).
ex: “The man whose dog I saw.”
الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي رَأَيْتُ كَلْبَهُ
“The two girls who are in the hotel.”
البِنْتانِ اللَّتانِ في الفُنْدُقِ
“I forgot the suitcase in the hotel (that) we are staying at.”
نَسِيتُ الحَقِيبَةَ في الفُنْدُقِ الَّذِي نُقِيمُ فِيهِ
“A man that we saw there.”
رَجُلٌ رَأَيْناهُ هُناكَ
“Whoever said that is a liar.”
مَنْ قالَ هذا فَهُوَ كَذّابٌ

sum: To ‘rise’ is to go up (ارْتَفَعَ); to ‘raise’ is to make something go up (رَفَعَ). A pay increase is a ‘rise’ (British) or a ‘raise’ (American).
ex: “The prices rose last week.”
ارْتَفَعَتِ الأَسْعارُ الأُسْبُوعَ الماضِي
“The government raised prices last week.”
رَفَعَتِ الحُكُومَةُ الأَسْعارَ الأُسْبُوعَ الماضِي

sum: ‘Say’ takes no personal object; ‘tell’ usually does. Arabic: قالَ (+ إِنَّ) for say; حَكَى, تَحَدَّثَ, حَدَّثَ, أَخْبَرَ for tell. Only ‘say’ can be followed directly by a ‘that’-clause.
ex: “He only said a few words to me.”
لَمْ يَتَحَدَّثْ مَعِي إِلّا قَلِيلاً
“He was telling me what (had) happened to his family during the war.”
كانَ يُخْبِرُنِي بِما حَصَلَ لِعائِلَتِهِ خِلالَ الحَرْبِ
“She said (NOT *told) that he was going home.”
قالَتْ إِنَّهُ كانَ ذاهِباً لِلْبَيْتِ

sum: English adds ‘-self’ to a pronoun; Arabic uses نَفْس (pl. أَنْفُس) with a suffix. As the first term of an iḍāfa, نَفْس means ‘same’.
pts: ذات renders ‘self’ in compounds: الثِّقَةُ بِالذّاتِ ‘self-confidence’, احْتِرامُ الذّاتِ ‘self-respect’, الحُكْمُ الذّاتِيُّ ‘self-determination’.
‘In itself’: في (حَدِّ) ذاتِهِ.
ex: “I can’t imagine myself in a world without paper, pens and books.”
لا أَتَصَوَّرُ نَفْسِي في عالَمٍ مِنْ دُونِ أَوْراقٍ وَأَقْلامٍ وَكُتُبٍ
“They, themselves, elected themselves.”
انْتَخَبُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ
“This crisis, in itself, is harmful to the national interest.”
هذِهِ الأَزْمَةُ في حَدِّ ذاتِها إِضْرارٌ بِالمَصالِحِ الوَطَنِيَّةِ

sum: ‘Sensible’ is about good judgement (حَصِيف, حَكِيم); ‘sensitive’ is about feeling (حَسّاس).
ex: “His father was a sensible man who realized the importance of education.”
كانَ أَبُوهُ رَجُلاً حَصِيفاً يَعْرِفُ أَهَمِّيَّةَ التَّعْلِيمِ
“Jojoba oil is excellent for people with sensitive skins.”
زَيْتُ الجُوجُوبا رائِعٌ خُصُوصاً لِلْأَشْخاصِ الَّذِينَ يُعانُونَ مِنْ جِلْدٍ حَسّاسٍ

sum: ‘Shade’ is a place out of the sun; a ‘shadow’ is the shape something casts. Arabic uses ظِلّ (pl. أَظْلال, ظِلال, ظُلُول) for both; a moving shadow of a person or animal can be شَبَح (pl. أَشْباح); figuratively, ظَلام also works.
pts: تَحْتَ / في ظِلِّ: ‘under the auspices of’, but في ظِلِّ can also mean ‘in (the) light of’.
تَقَلَّصَ ظِلُّهُ ‘his authority dwindled’; وِزارَةُ الظِّلِّ ‘shadow cabinet’.
ex: “I noticed a shadow moving outside the bedroom.”
لاحَظْتُ شَبَحاً مُتَحَرِّكاً خارِجَ غُرْفَةِ النَّوْمِ
“Diplomacy should take place in the light of day, not in the shadows.”
تَجْدُرُ مُمارَسَةُ الدِّبْلُوماسِيَّةِ في النُّورِ وَلَيْسَ في الظَّلامِ
“The project was completed under the auspices of the UN.”
تَمَّ المَشْرُوعُ تَحْتَ ظِلِّ الأُمَمِ المُتَّحِدَةِ

sum: ‘Some’ is for affirmative sentences, ‘any’ for questions and negatives. Arabic uses بَعْض (in an iḍāfa or with a suffix) and أَيّ. ‘Some’ and ‘some of’ are both بَعْض, without مِنْ.
pts: ‘Some’ and ‘any’ are often not translated at all, especially with ‘there was/were’.
‘Any’ meaning ‘whatever’: أَيّ … كانَ in the perfect (بِأَيَّةِ صِفَةٍ كانَتْ ‘in any capacity’).
‘In any case’ (anyway): عَلَى / في كُلِّ حالٍ.
ex: ‘some (of the) ministers’
بَعْضُ الوُزَراءِ (NOT *بَعْضٌ مِنَ الوُزَراءِ)
“I’ll bring you some coffee in a minute.”
سَوْفَ أُحْضِرُ لَكَ فِنْجاناً مِنَ القَهْوَةِ خِلالَ دَقِيقَةٍ
“There weren’t any tourists in the church.”
لَمْ يَكُنْ هُناكَ أَيُّ سائِحٍ في الكَنِيسَةِ

sum: ‘Sometimes’ means now and then (أَحْياناً); ‘sometime’ means at one time, formerly (سابِقاً). ‘Sometimes … sometimes’ is تارَةً … تارَةً, تارَةً … طَوْراً, or تارَةً … (تارَةً) أُخْرَى.
ex: “He was a sometime professor at Harvard.”
كانَ أُسْتاذاً في جامِعَةِ هارْفارْد سابِقاً
“Sometimes/at times she chides me, other times she turns to me for help.”
تَلُومُنِي تارَةً وَتارَةً تَتَوَسَّلُنِي

ar: ما زال / حتى الآن / مع ذلك
sum: ‘Still’ changes meaning with context. ‘As before, now or in future’: ما زالَ / لا يَزالُ + adjective, accusative noun or imperfect. ‘Until now’: حَتَّى / إِلَى الآنَ. ‘Yet, however’: مَعَ أَنَّ, مَعَ ذلِكَ.
ex: “It was still difficult.”
ما زالَ صَعْباً
“She still loves me.”
لا تَزالُ تُحِبُّنِي
“I still don’t know his name.”
لا أَعْرِفُ اسْمَهُ حَتَّى الآنَ
“The newspaper apologized about the mistakes in the article, but he still sued them.”
اعْتَذَرَتِ الجَرِيدَةُ لَهُ عَنِ الأَخْطاءِ في المَقالَةِ وَمَعَ ذلِكَ رَفَعَ عَلَيْها دَعْوَى

sum: The English subjunctive is the bare infinitive for all persons (or, in formal British English, should + infinitive) after verbs and phrases of demand, advice or necessity (advise, ask, demand, insist, propose, recommend, request, suggest, urge; it is best, crucial, essential, imperative, important, vital that). The Arabic subjunctive shares the name but little else.
pts: Arabic uses it after purpose particles (لِـ, كَيْ, لِكَيْ, حَتَّى: ‘in order to, so that’), after لَنْ (negative future), and after أَنْ with verbs of desire, intention and need.
ex: “It is imperative that you be there.”
عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَكُونَ هُناكَ
“They demanded (that) the government release the leader of the party.”
طالَبُوا الحُكُومَةَ بِإِطْلاقِ سَراحِ زَعِيمِ الحِزْبِ
“So that the international community takes its responsibilities.”
لِكَيْ يَتَحَمَّلَ المُجْتَمَعُ الدَّوْلِيُّ مَسْؤُولِيّاتِهِ

sum: Arabic has no English-style derivational suffixes, so there is never a one-to-one match. The usual solutions are an iḍāfa (‘presidency’, مُدَّةُ الرِّئاسَةِ) or a noun phrase (‘infallible’, مُنَزَّهٌ عَنِ الخَطَإِ; ‘drinkable’, قابِلٌ لِلشُّرْبِ).

Address is culture-bound. Arabic has more honorifics and uses them more widely, and first names on first meeting can seem disrespectful. Translate according to context, the relationship between the people and what the speaker intends: tone honorifics down or drop them into English, add them into Arabic.
pts: حَضْرَتُكَ is sometimes ‘sir’ but usually just ‘you’.
Titles such as حاجّ or أُسْتاذ appear even when the person is no pilgrim or teacher.
Arabic puts a title before the first name, English before the surname: الدُّكْتُورَةُ سارَة is ‘Dr Johnson’, not ‘Dr Sarah’.

Formulas for the dead (المَرْحُومُ before the name, رَحِمَهُ اللهُ after) are translated once and then dropped; رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ after the Companions is omitted. صَلَّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ (‘PBUH’) suits texts for a Muslim readership, not general media.

rows: His Highness Shaykh …, the Minister for …
His Royal Highness / His Excellency / His Majesty / Your Excellency

ex: “Dr Johnson agreed on this matter.” (NOT *‘Dr Sarah…’)
وافَقَتِ الدُّكْتُورَةُ سارَة عَلَى هذا الأَمْرِ
“Excuse me sir, where is the entrance(, please)?”
يا أُسْتاذُ، أَيْنَ المَدْخَلُ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ؟

sum: Arabic has no present copula, so ‘there is/are’ depends on tense, sentence type and whether a place is named.
pts: Present: affirmative هُناكَ / هُنالِكَ; questions with هَلْ / أَ; negative لَيْسَ; negative question أَلَيْسَ. Add هُناكَ when no place is given.
Past: كانَ (subject nominative, predicate accusative); questions هَلْ / أَ كانَ; negative لَمْ يَكُنْ (there has not been) or ما كانَ (there wasn’t); أَلَمْ يَكُنْ for negative questions.
Future: سَيَكُونُ; negative لَنْ يَكُونَ; أَسَيَكُونُ, أَلَنْ يَكُونَ.
If the place is ‘there’, Arabic puts هُناكَ at the end, while English repeats ‘there’.
كانَ هُناكَ دَلْوٌ ‘There was a bucket’ differs from كانَ دَلْواً ‘It was a bucket’.
English often adds ‘any’ in negatives and questions, and uses ‘no’ rather than ‘not’.
ex: “There is a school in the centre of town.”
هُناكَ / هُنالِكَ مَدْرَسَةٌ في وَسَطِ المَدِينَةِ
“Is there no coffee?”
أَلَيْسَتْ هُناكَ / هُنالِكَ قَهْوَةٌ؟
“There were no/have not been any newspapers in the waiting room.”
لَمْ تَكُنْ هُناكَ جَرائِدُ في غُرْفَةِ الانْتِظارِ
“There will not be (any) money in the bank.”
لَنْ تَكُونَ هُناكَ أَمْوالٌ في المَصْرِفِ
“Is there no coffee there?”
أَلَيْسَتْ قَهْوَةٌ هُناكَ؟

sum: ‘Time’ has several Arabic equivalents depending on the sense.
pts: Abstract: زَمَن (pl. أَزْمان), or تَوْقِيت (‘summer time’, ‘GMT’).
A point or period: وَقْت (pl. أَوْقات); an appointed time: تَوْقِيت, مِيقات (pl. مَواقِيت). An English plural may be an Arabic singular and vice versa.
Era, age, epoch: عَصْر (pl. عُصُور, أَعْصُر, أَعْصار), دَهْر (pl. دُهُور; also a very long time), زَمَن, زَمان, وَقْت. زَمَن is also grammatical ‘tense’.
One occurrence: مَرَّة.

Expressions: كَمِ السّاعَةُ؟ ‘What’s the time?’; عَلَى مَرِّ الزَّمانِ ‘in the course of time’; حانَ وَقْتُ الذَّهابِ ‘it’s time to go’; قَضَيْنا وَقْتاً مُمْتِعاً ‘we had a good time’; المَرَّةُ القادِمَةُ ‘next time’; مَرَّةً بَعْدَ مَرَّةٍ ‘time and again’.
As a verb: ‘to time a race’ (دَوَّنَ / سَجَّلَ وَقْتَ), ‘He timed the attack perfectly.’
ex: “Time was one of the things that occupied people’s minds.”
إِنَّ الزَّمَنَ مِنَ الأَشْياءِ الَّتي شَغَلَتْ فِكْرَ الإِنْسانِ
“The post office opening times during Ramadan are from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m.”
مَواقِيتُ / أَوْقاتُ عَمَلِ مَكاتِبِ البَرِيدِ في شَهْرِ رَمَضانَ مِنَ الثّامِنَةِ صَباحاً إِلَى الخامِسَةِ مَساءً
“He has lived in exile for a long time/for ages.”
أَقامَ في بِلادِ الغُرْبَةِ دَهْراً
“This time, I’ll forgive him.”
سَأَغْفِرُ لَهُ هذِهِ المَرَّةَ

ar: جداً / أكثر من اللازم / أفرط في
sum: No single Arabic word matches ‘too’. The usual solutions are the elative meaning ‘more than necessary’ (أَكْثَرُ مِنَ اللّازِمِ, أَكْثَرُ مِمّا يَنْبَغِي, أَكْثَرُ مِمّا يَجِبُ), the verb أَفْرَطَ في + noun, or the adverb جِدّاً.
pts: ‘Too + adjective + for/to + infinitive’ becomes an elative + مِنْ + أَنْ: ‘too young to vote’, أَصْغَرُ سِنّاً مِنْ أَنْ يُدْلِيَ بِصَوْتِهِ.
English needs ‘too difficult a task’, not *‘too difficult task’.
Arabic speakers often misuse ‘too’ as a plain intensifier (*‘He loves her too much’ meaning ‘very much’).
Idioms: ‘It’s not too bad’ (هُوَ بَيْنَ بَيْنَ); ‘It’s too good to be true’ (أَغْرَبُ مِنْ أَنْ يُصَدَّقَ).
ex: “He drinks too much.”
يُفْرِطُ في الشَّرابِ
“She talked too much.”
تَكَلَّمَتْ أَكْثَرَ مِمّا يَنْبَغِي
“The circumstances were too sensitive to be mentioned.”
كانَتِ الظُّرُوفُ أَكْثَرَ حَساسِيَّةً مِنْ أَنْ نَسْتَطِيعَ الكَلامَ عَنْها
“This is too difficult a task for us to do.”
هذِهِ المُهِمَّةُ أَصْعَبُ مِنْ أَنْ نَقُومَ بِها

sum: There is no single agreed system for writing Arabic in Latin letters (romanization). Transliteration is strictly letter for letter; transcription renders sounds. Scholarly forms (Najīb Maḥfūẓ) and everyday ones (Naguib Mahfouz, Nagib Machfus, Nadjib Mahfoez) can look like different people. Choose by audience and be consistent.
pts: Unicode guidance says a system should be standard, complete, predictable, pronounceable and reversible; no common Arabic system manages all five.
Narrow (scholarly): ء ’, ث th, ج j, ح ḥ, خ kh, ذ dh, ش sh, ص ṣ, ض ḍ, ط ṭ, ظ ẓ, ع ‘, غ gh, ق q; long vowels ā ī ū; diphthongs ay, aw.

ة is -a, but -at in the first term of an iḍāfa (mudarrisa, mudarrisat al-kulliyya); nisba -ī / -iyya; tanwīn usually dropped (except set words like jiddan); doubled consonants written twice (dubb); no assimilation (al-shams); hyphen after the article (al-qamar); Western numerals; bi ’l-qalam after a vowel; capitalize Al- at the start of a sentence.
Use naturalized forms: imam, not imām, just as ‘taco’ or ‘bikini’ are now English.
Colloquial: transcribe the actual sound (Egyptian nagm for najm; Palestinian al-’uds), with e, o, ē, ō if needed.
Broad (for general readers), in order: (1) a recognized form if there is one, (2) the form closest to the Arabic (Ahmad, not Ahmed), (3) fewer letters (Hasan, not Hassan), (4) consistency.

Proper names: do not translate them (Ibrahim stays Ibrahim, not Abraham), but use an established English form if one exists (سارة → Sarah); for names originally English or French, restore the original (ميشال → Michel), while ميخائيل stays Mikha’il. Historic Spanish place names keep their Arabic forms: طُلَيْطِلَة Toledo, قُرْطُبَة Cordoba, الحَمْراء Alhambra.

English into Arabic: forms vary (غواتيمالا / جواتيمالا; شارل / تشارلز); short vowels are lengthened (دانيال), consonant clusters are allowed (شنغهاي), emphatics are frequent (قُنْصُل). Put the foreign name in brackets the first time, and in technical texts give the Latin-script form as well.
ex: Common Arabic names, broad forms
عبد الرحمن ’Abd ar-Rahman · عبد الله ’Abdullah · عادل ’Adil, Adel · حسن Hasan · حسين Husayn, Hussein · محمد Muhammad · مصطفى Mustafa · يوسف Yusuf, Youssef · زينب Zaynab, Zeinab
“Professor Andy Smith wrote an article on internal medicine.”
كَتَبَ البُرُوفِسُور (أَنْدِي سْمِيث) مَقالَةً حَوْلَ الأَمْراضِ الباطِنِيَّةِ

sum: ‘Until’ (informally ‘till’) is for an ongoing state; ‘by’ is for something done at or before a point. Arabic: حَتَّى (+ genitive) or إِلَى for until, قَبْلَ for by.
pts: حَتَّى also means ‘up to (and including)’, close to بِما في ذلِكَ ‘including’; ‘in order to’ with the subjunctive; and ‘even’.
ex: “We’ll stay here until the evening.”
سَنَبْقَى هُنا حَتَّى المَساءِ
“I hope you will be able to do it by Friday.”
آمُلُ أَنْ تَعْمَلَهُ قَبْلَ يَوْمِ الجُمْعَةِ
“The investigators searched the building from the basement up to (including) the roof.”
فَتَّشَ المُحَقِّقُونَ المَبْنَى مِنَ السِّرْدابِ حَتَّى السَّقْفِ

sum: Both can mean ‘and’ but are not interchangeable. Only فَـ introduces the result of a condition; only وَ introduces a circumstantial clause (حال); وَ is the one used between nouns (English uses commas and one ‘and’ before the last item).
pts: فَـ links cause and effect or a sequence (also ثُمَّ, وَبَعْدَ ذلِكَ, وَبَعْدَهُ): ‘and so’, ‘thus’, ‘as a result’, ‘therefore’.
فَـ can be contrastive: ‘yet’, ‘however’.
ex: “I saw Salwa, Leila and Sally.”
رَأَيْتُ سَلْوَى وَلَيْلَى وَسالِي (NOT فَلَيْلَى)
“He failed the exam and (so he) had to leave the university.”
فَشِلَ في الامْتِحانِ فَيَجِبُ أَنْ يَتْرُكَ الجامِعَةَ
“Her accomplice confessed, yet she insists on denying her involvement.”
رُغْمَ اعْتِرافِ شَرِيكِها فَهِيَ تَنْفِي تَوَرُّطَها بِإِلْحاحٍ

sum: Both appear in conditionals, but ‘when’ implies certainty. Arabic: إِذا (or لَوْ) for ‘if’; لَمّا or حِينَ for ‘when’.
ex: “If he gets here [not certain], I shall tell him what happened.”
إِذا جاءَ فَأَحْكِي لَهُ ما حَصَلَ
“When he becomes managing director [certain], he will make a few changes.”
لَمّا يُصْبِحُ مُدِيراً تَتَغَيَّرُ بَعْضُ الأَشْياءِ

sum: Meaning ‘irrespective of’, it is rendered by لَوْ كانَ … أَوْ / أَمْ, إِنْ كانَ … أَوْ / أَمْ, سَواءٌ كانَ … أَوْ / أَمْ, and sometimes a simple coordinator.
ex: “There is no such thing as unimportant art, whether it be locally or internationally.”
لا يُوجَدُ فَنٌّ بِلا أَهَمِّيَّةٍ سَواءٌ كانَ مَحَلِّيّاً أَوْ عالَمِيّاً
“He will do it, whether he wants/likes to or not (willy-nilly).”
سَيَعْمَلُ غَصْباً أَمْ طَوْعاً / مِنْ غَيْرِ غَصْبٍ

sum: Both mark contrast and are often interchangeable, but only ‘while’ also expresses simultaneity. Arabic: في حِينِ (أَنَّ), عَلَى / في حِينِ أَنَّ, بَيْنَما (also simultaneous), حَيْثُ.
ex: “Foreign forces liberated the South, whereas/while the North was freed by domestic resistants.”
تَوَلَّتِ القُوّاتُ الأَجْنَبِيَّةُ تَحْرِيرَ الجَنُوبِ عَلَى حِينِ أَنَّ الشَّمالَ تَحَرَّرَ عَلَى يَدِ مُقاوِمِي الدّاخِلِ
“He was reading while she was cooking dinner.”
كانَ يَقْرَأُ بَيْنَما كانَتْ تُعِدُّ العَشاءَ

sum: Traditionally ‘shall’ was for the first person and ‘will’ for the others; formal usage no longer keeps this, and both contract to ’ll. In legal English, ‘shall’ expresses obligation with the second and third persons.
ex: “We shall/’ll be here.”
سَنَكُونُ هُنا
“The employee shall be deemed to have been appointed under probation for three months.”
يُعْتَبَرُ المُوَظَّفُ مُعَيَّناً تَحْتَ الاخْتِبارِ لِمُدَّةِ ثَلاثَةِ شُهُورٍ

sum: ‘Wish’ takes many constructions: + to + infinitive, + clause, + that, + pronoun, + for. With a past or present reference, the hypothetical past (subjunctive) marks something unreal; with a future reference, a possibility.
pts: Arabic can render it as hypothetical ‘if only …’ (لَوْ, ‘would that’) or as ‘like’ or ‘want’.
Verbs: رَغِبَ في (+ أَنْ before a verb), تَمَنَّى, اشْتاقَ, رَجا, ارْتَجَى; they also cover ‘hope’, ‘look forward to’, ‘want’. Watch the prepositions Arabic needs and English does not.
ex: “I wish you were here.”
أَتَمَنَّى لَوْ كُنْتَ هُناكَ
“I wish we knew how much they were making on the deal.”
أَوَدُّ لَوْ عَرَفْنا كَمْ سَيَكْسِبُونَ مِنْ هذِهِ الصَّفْقَةِ
“If only I knew/had known about his fraud …”
لَوْ كُنْتُ قَدْ عَرَفْتُ / أَعْرِفُ عَنِ احْتِيالِهِ
“Israel wishes to obtain US assistance to implement its project.”
تَرْغَبُ إِسْرائِيلُ في الحُصُولِ عَلَى مُساعَدَةِ الوِلاياتِ المُتَّحِدَةِ مِنْ أَجْلِ تَطْبِيقِ خُطَطِها
